items.title: U.S. stocks slip following a discouraging update on inflation
items.description: The U.S. stock market dipped Tuesday after a report showed inflation was worse across the country last month than economists expected.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Traders work on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange in New York, Monday, July 6, 2026. (AP Photo/Seth Wenig)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Seth Wenig</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: The U.S. stock market dipped Tuesday after a report showed inflation was worse across the country last month than economists expected.
items.body:
NEW YORK — The U.S. stock market dipped Tuesday after a report showed inflation was worse across the country last month than economists expected.

The S&P 500 slipped 0.4 per cent and gave back some of its big rally from the day before. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 157 points, or 0.3 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite sank 0.7 per cent.

Pressure from the bond market undercut stocks following the discouraging report on inflation. People had to pay prices for groceries, electricity and other costs of living that were higher last month than economists expected. That could push the Federal Reserve to hike its main interest rate at its next meeting in December and beyond.

  • S&P 500 market updates here

Higher interest rates can help rein in inflation, but they do so by making it more expensive for everyone to borrow money and by slowing the overall economy. Higher rates also make investors less willing to pay high prices for stocks and other investments.

One Fed official even hinted the central bank may increase the federal funds rate by double the typical amount next month because of how high inflation has remained for years.

Speaking in London before the inflation report was released, Fed Gov. Christopher Waller said “a stronger policy move may be needed” if the report showed an important underlying measure of inflation rose by 0.3 per cent from September.

In that case, he said the Fed should consider hiking the federal funds rate by half a percentage point rather than the typical quarter point. Moving by only the usual amount could “put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take.”

Shortly afterward, Tuesday’s inflation report showed that the underlying measure of inflation Waller was worried about was exactly 0.3 per cent, the threshold he had set. It’s the Fed’s job to keep inflation under control, along with keeping the job market strong.

That sent yields jumping in the bond market as traders upped their forecasts for coming hikes to rates by the Fed.

The yield on the 10-year Treasury leaped to 4.99 per cent from 4.88 per cent late Monday. It’s a notable move for the bond market, and the yield helps set where rates are for mortgages and other loans going to U.S. households and businesses.

The 10-year Treasury yield had been dropping since early October, when it topped 5.30 per cent as worries spiked about high inflation, higher interest rates, the U.S. government’s big debt and other concerns.

Tuesday’s jump in yields came even though oil prices fell again. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil fell 1.2 per cent to US$91.49. President Donald Trump said late Monday that the war in Iran, which sent oil prices much higher, “militarily is effectively over.”

Brent’s price has been falling from more than US$112 at the start of the month amid uncertainty about what will happen with the war with Iran.

  • Stay on top of your portfolio with real-time data, historical charts and the latest news on oil

Jumps in Treasury yields push downward on prices for all kinds of stocks, and they can particularly hurt companies in the real-estate business.

Higher mortgage rates can keep potential customers away from homebuilders, for example, and Lennar fell 5.4 per cent for one of the sharper losses in the S&P 500.

Rival homebuilders also fell, including drops of 3.8 per cent for D.R. Horton and 3.9 per cent for PulteGroup. Builders FirstSource, which sells crown mouldings, cabinets and other products to homebuilders, sank 4.6 per cent.

The single heaviest weight on the S&P 500 was Nvidia, which fell 5.5 per cent. It’s been under pressure since its board announced an investigation into its CEO, Jensen Huang, who admitted to a relationship with a woman who, according to The New York Times, U.S. intelligence determined was gathering information for China.

It’s also been swinging amid broader worries that have knocked the artificial-intelligence industry around recently. Democratic victories in statehouses across the country last week raised concerns about possible restrictions on construction of AI data centres. That built on top of longstanding worries that AI stock prices had shot too high and were in a bubble.

GE Vernova, which is helping to power AI data centres, dropped 3.9 per cent. Micron Technology, which sells memory for computers, fell 1.1 per cent. CoreWeave, a company that rents out access to AI chips to customers over the cloud, slipped 0.5 per cent.

Other AI-related stocks held up better, though. Broadcom climbed 3.9 per cent, and Advanced Micro Devices rose 1.3 per cent.

The recent shakiness for AI-related stocks had raised questions about whether Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, may delay its initial public offering of stock.

  • Latest updates on investing here

But Anthropic said in a filing with U.S. regulators on Tuesday that it’s looking to sell its stock at a price valuing the company at roughly US$1.3 trillion. That would make it one of the most valuable companies on Wall Street, worth more than Walmart, JPMorgan Chase, ExxonMobil or Coca-Cola.

All told, the S&P 500 fell 29.01 points to 7,520.93. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 157.86 to 52,231.89, and the Nasdaq composite sank 187.26 to 25,065.87.

In stock markets abroad, indexes rose across much of Europe and Asia.

South Korea’s Kospi jumped 4.4 per cent for one of the world’s biggest gains on strength for its two tech giants that have benefited from the AI boom, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix.

Stan Choe, The Associated Press

AP Writers Elaine Lai and Matt Ott contributed to this report

items.title: Ottawa puts sharper focus on permanent residency for privately sponsored refugees
items.description: The federal government is increasing the number of privately sponsored refugees eligible for permanent residency in the coming years as it reduces the number of eligible government-sponsored refugees.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[The Peace tower is seen on Parliament Hill in Ottawa, Monday, Sept. 21, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Adrian Wyld]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Adrian Wyld</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: The federal government is increasing the number of privately sponsored refugees eligible for permanent residency in the coming years as it reduces the number of eligible government-sponsored refugees.
items.body:
The federal government is increasing the number of privately sponsored refugees eligible for permanent residency in the coming years as it reduces the number of eligible government-sponsored refugees.

The 2027 immigration levels plan, released last week, says about 29,000 refugees and another 20,000 protected persons and family members will be granted permanent residency status annually through 2029.

Overall, the number is similar to last year but within that number, the government is making adjustments to who is eligible for permanent residency.

The number of privately sponsored refugees eligible will increase to 17,500 from 16,000 last year, while the number of eligible government-sponsored refugees will fall to just under 12,000 from more than 13,000 in 2025.

Groups, such as religious societies and community organizations, that privately sponsor refugees help them find housing and provide them with food, rent, clothing and other essentials during their first year in Canada.

Renze Nauta, a program director for the non-partisan think tank Cardus, said increasing the number of privately sponsored refugees is a good idea because they tend to be more successful at integration than those who are aided by the government.

Nauta said Cardus wrote Immigration Minister Lena Diab in September asking that the percentage of privately sponsored refugees be increased after it was reduced last year.

“I think this is an example of where governments do leverage civil society and Canadians who support them, and I think we should do more of that,” he said.

But Lauren Lallemand, co-executive director of the Canadian Council for Refugees, said the shift to privately sponsored refugees suggests the government is off-loading its responsibility onto civil society groups.

“The government has a moral and international law obligation to resettle refugees,” Lallemand said.

“We’re disappointed to see what we interpret as a further kind of reduction in the state’s ownership of their responsibility in making sure that people receive protection in Canada and basically just transferring it on to communities and members of civil society.”

Nauta said there is evidence privately sponsored refugees do better at settling in because they receive more direct, personalized support.

“That will allow for a growth in immigration if that’s what the government calls for later on,” he said. “But it does start with that integration. That’s hard to do but Canadians have shown for the last several decades that they’re willing to do it, they have the heart to do, it and they have the means.”

Citing declining rates of newcomers — including refugees — since 2024, both Prime Minister Mark Carney and Immigration Minister Lena Diab have argued the immigration system is back under control.

Lallemand said it’s disconcerting to hear the government point to declining numbers of refugees as part of its immigration narrative.

“There are several global crises happening now that mean that there are far more displaced people than there were even 10 years ago, for example, or 15 years ago,” she said.

“The acceptance rate for refugees who apply through asylum is quite high. It’s above 70 per cent. And so kind of implying that you are getting immigration under control by further blocking people from accessing safety is very troubling.”

The government passed a law last year that says conventional asylum claims must be filed within a year of the claimant’s first arrival in Canada. Those applying after that time can still obtain protection through a pre-removal risk assessment — the appeal mechanism for a rejected asylum claim.

The government has justified the new power by pointing to a major spike in asylum claims after the COVID-19 pandemic — a spike that included people using the system to extend their time in Canada when their visas were set to expire.

items.body:
OTTAWA — The federal government has released a list of the private sector companies lending staff to the major projects office after initially refusing to do so.

Conservative and Bloc Québécois MPs have for months pressed Ottawa to reveal the list, citing concerns about conflicts of interest.

A copy of the list obtained by The Canadian Press, first reported on by The Toronto Star, shows nine employees from the Bank of Montreal, two from RBC and one from Scotiabank.

The list also includes four staffers from the Government of Yukon and one each from the governments of British Columbia and the Northwest Territories.

Major projects office officials have insisted their employees are not in conflicts and that they’ve been cleared by human resources in the Privy Council Office.

Federal Energy Minister Tim Hodgson dismissed calls for the list last week and accused opposition MPs of peddling “conspiracy theories.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 10, 2026.

Canadian meal delivery company Fresh Prep Foods Inc. says it has received court permission to acquire distressed competitor Goodfood Market Corp.

Fresh Prep refused to disclose how much it will pay for Goodfood but says the deal is expected to close on or around Friday.

Once the deal closes, Fresh Prep says it will begin serving about 30,000 Goodfood customers.

  • Latest updates on company news here

Goodfood filed for creditor protection with the Superior Court of Quebec over the summer in hopes of restructuring under a new owner or with help from investors.

The Montreal-based company started in 2014 and is known for selling pre-measured sets of ingredients and recipes to customers who cook them into meals.

Fresh Prep operates similarly. It was founded in Vancouver in 2015 and acquired another Montreal-based meal kit company called Cook It Recipes Inc. in 2024.

items.title: ‘A betrayal:’ Carney says Canada will ‘fully enforce’ its rights following sale of Stellantis plant
items.description: Prime Minister Mark Carney says that a decision by automaker Stellantis to sell its Brampton assembly plant amounts to a “betrayal” of thousands of workers.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Prime Minister Mark Carney and the idled Stellantis assembly plant in Brampton, Ont., in a combination photo. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Graham Hughes/Arlyn McAdorey]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: Prime Minister Mark Carney says that a decision by automaker Stellantis to sell its Brampton assembly plant amounts to a “betrayal” of thousands of workers.
items.body:
Prime Minister Mark Carney says that a decision by automaker Stellantis to sell its Brampton, Ont., assembly plant amounts to a “betrayal” of thousands of workers.

Carney made the comment during a press conference in Montreal on Tuesday, one day after Stellantis announced that it would sell the idle plant to Canadian armoured vehicle manufacturer Roshel.

More than 2,200 workers have been on layoff at the Brampton plant since production was halted in December 2023.

During an interview with CP24 Breakfast earlier on Tuesday, the CEO of Roshel said that while his company will prioritize Brampton residents in hiring it “is not going to even consider” taking on any responsibility for rehiring all Stellantis workers.

“The situation at the Brampton plant is unacceptable. It violates the obligations that Stellantis has under several agreements. But to be more fundamental it is a betrayal of the workers as it is a betrayal of the obligations to Canada and by extension to all Canadians,” Carney said on Tuesday. “We will fully enforce our rights in protection of those workers and in protection of Canadian funds.”

In May 2022, the federal government agreed to provide Stellantis with $529 million in funding to retool its Brampton and Windsor plants.

In a statement to CTV News on Tuesday, Stellantis said that it has “offered to voluntarily return the government support received for Brampton Assembly’s original retooling plan,” though it said that it cannot disclose the total amount.

Appearing alongside Carney in Montreal, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said that she will be meeting with officials from Unifor and Stellantis in Toronto on Thursday to discuss a path forward.

Joly had previously said that the decision by Stellantis to sell the plant “does not erase the commitments they made to workers in Brampton.”

“For more than a year we have been engaging with Stellantis, engaging with Unifor, trying to find a solution for Brampton but Stellantis has decided to go ahead and violate its contract, so that is why, as the prime minister has said, we will use the full force of the law to make sure we protect jobs but also bring justice to these workers that are waiting to just get a job from their employer, which is Stellantis,” Joly said.

‘A much brighter future’

There is a long history of manufacturing at the Brampton assembly plant dating back to 1986.

Most recently, the Dodge Charger and Dodge Challenger were assembled in Brampton but the last of those vehicles rolled off the assembly line in 2023.

At the time, Stellantis said that the plant would undergo improvements to begin manufacturing electric vehicles.

In an interview with CP24 Breakfast on Tuesday, Roshel CEO Roman Shimonov promised a “much brighter” future for the Brampton plant once the deal with Stellantis closes later this year.

“We are talking about an idle plant that wasn’t operating for many years and now we have a new, much brighter future. People that criticized (the sale), they either haven’t been briefed on the facts or are just ignoring them because we are talking about a plant that was idled for many years,” he said.

Shimonov has said that Roshel will look to create thousands of jobs in Brampton but the company has provided few specific details beyond saying that they want to bring a new “centre of excellence for advanced manufacturing” to the former Stellantis site.

In an interview with CTV News Channel on Tuesday, Automotive Parts Manufacturing Association president Flavio Volpe said that the Brampton assembly plant was at one point responsible for thousands of direct jobs and an estimated 10,000 to 12,000 additional jobs at parts suppliers plants.

He predicted that the jobs created by an armoured vehicle manufacturing facility would be a fraction of that.

“He (Shimonov) is standing in and saying, ‘well I can do that.’ Well, you can’t do that. We know you can’t do that,” Volpe said, explaining that many of the armoured vehicles manufactured by Roshel are made using chassis imported from the U.S.

“The difference for your viewers, you think about a hot rod shop or your local mechanic who is doing work on several vehicles a day versus something as big as the Eaton Centre, if not bigger, full with 1,000 vehicles a day and thousands of employees. Making them, shipping them out and doing another 1,000 tomorrow. It is scales different and it is embarrassing that we are even pretending that it’s the same.”

Roshel won’t commit to rehiring workers

Shimonov was asked by CP24 Breakfast whether he would commit to rehiring impacted workers but said that is not something he is willing to do.

He also said that Roshel will not be involved in any negotiations that may take place between Unifor, the federal government and Stellantis.

“I can confirm that we will give a priority to people in Brampton the way we always do. We are in Brampton and there is a reason we are in Brampton. Brampton is an amazing place to develop and to create a competitive business, but a competitive business cannot work by taking obligations of other companies and we are not going to even consider taking any responsibilities of anyone from previous engagements,” Shimonov said.

Tories call for Joly’s job

Unifor has accused Stellantis of betraying its members with an “underhanded deal” that allows it to “walk away from its commitments.”

During a press conference outside the plant on Tuesday, federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre called the impending sale “yet another Liberal betrayal of Canada’s working people.”

Poilievre said that despite promises of new jobs, the reality is that Canadian jobs are moving to the U.S. with “nothing but vague promises of a smaller number of jobs for an undefined group of workers.”

The Conservative leader added that he wants the Carney government to launch a lawsuit against Stellantis “to get Canadian tax dollars back.” Separately, he is calling on Carney to fire Joly over her handling of the Stellantis file.

“We need to know the exact sum, every penny that has gone to Stellantis for all of its operations in Canada under this Liberal government and we need every penny to be repaid. Until that happens, we will not relent because our mission is to save money and jobs,” Poilievre said.

items._ogDesc: The Bank of Canada’s governing council thinks it might need to raise interest rates further, but it’s proceeding carefully, according to a summary of deliberations.
items.body:
OTTAWA — The Bank of Canada’s governing council thinks it might need to raise interest rates further, but it’s proceeding carefully, according to a summary of deliberations of its recent decision to raise its key policy rate for the first time since 2023.

According to the report, the council acknowledged it faced considerable uncertainty and said it would take its monetary policy decisions one meeting at a time.

The Bank of Canada raised its policy interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 2.5 per cent last month to reduce the risk that stubbornly high oil prices become persistent inflation.

  • Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.ca

The summary says the council members agreed that monetary policy cannot lower global energy prices, but can prevent them from leading to generalized inflation.

The decision came as the Bank of Canada raised its outlook for the annual inflation rate to hit 3.5 per cent at the end of this year and remain above three per cent for much of 2027.

The summary of deliberations said higher costs largely haven’t been passed through to consumers so far, but the bank’s surveys suggest businesses expect to raise some prices over the next year.

items._ogDesc: Top Picks from Christine Poole, President & Co-Chief Investment Officer, Davis Rea
items.body:
Christine Poole, President & Co-Chief Investment Officer, Davis Rea

Focus: North American Large Caps

Top Picks: Microsoft, RTX Corp, Stryker

In October, the contrast in performance between the headline S&P 500 Index and the S&P 500 Equal Weight Index highlighted a significant broadening in market breadth. The market cap weighted index was down 0.9 per cent in the month while the equal weighted index was up 4.9 per cent. Broadening market breadth means the participation in a stock market rally is expanding beyond a concentrated handful of mega-cap technology companies to include a wider variety of companies across diverse sectors. The Democratic sweep in the midterm elections has added uncertainty to the pace of the AI buildout and put additional downward pressure on AI-related stocks.

The resilient U.S. economy continues to expand, supported by strength in consumer spending and private business AI-related investment. U.S GDP grew by 2.2 per cent in the second quarter and accelerated to 3.4 per cent in the third quarter. The unemployment rate is low, hovering around four per cent. Leading economic indicators reinforce durable momentum with the ISM Manufacturing Purchasing Managers Index (PMI) signaling expansion for ten consecutive months, and the Services PMI expanding for 28 consecutive months. However, inflation continues to be stubbornly above the Federal Reserve’s long-term two per cent target, serving as the primary reason for the central bank’s September rate hike.

The Canadian economy is expanding at a more modest pace, anchored by subdued consumer spending, muted population growth, and ongoing trade-related pressures. According to the Bank of Canada’s latest Monetary Policy report, GDP is expected to be two per cent in the third quarter and slow to below one per cent in the fourth quarter. The unemployment rate has been around 6.5 per cent, pointing to excess supply in the economy. While core inflation (excluding gasoline) remains close to two per cent, the Bank of Canada increased interest rates in October as a preventative measure in anticipation of increased cost pass-through as higher energy prices and tariff-related costs are eventually priced into consumer goods and services.

Looking ahead to next year, economic growth in Canada is projected to improve due to stronger business investment, bolstered by federal tax incentives such as the Productivity Mega Deduction, and government spending. The long-term sustainability of spending in AI and continued growth in consumer spending, which accounts for about 70 per cent of U.S.

GDP, are key drivers for continued U.S. economic prosperity. A caveat to a slower pace of AI investment is reduced inflationary pressures for technology goods.

Our investment framework shifts away from market timing and toward what we can control: owning reasonably priced, high-quality companies within industries that offer attractive secular growth or stable income generation. Staying invested in a diversified portfolio with an asset mix geared to your risk tolerance and financial capacity is the path to preserving and generating long-term wealth.

Microsoft (MSFT NASD)

Microsoft is a global technology company providing a wide range of software services and products including Windows, Office 365, LinkedIn, and Azure cloud computing as well as owning a leading gaming platform, Xbox, and video game publisher, Activision Blizzard. Its growing recurring revenue, robust cloud computing growth, and strong balance sheet are appealing investment attributes. Microsoft’s dividend yield is 0.7 per cent.

RTX is a aerospace and defense company engaged in providing advanced systems and services for commercial, military and government customers. Its product portfolio includes avionics, interiors, aircraft engines, sensor and communication systems and missile defense systems. Its commercial aerospace businesses benefit from the growth in global air travel while demand for its defense products is robust due to ongoing geopolitical conflicts. The stock provides a dividend yield of 1.5 per cent.

Stryker is a leading medical technology company offering a broad portfolio of products and services across neurotechnology and orthopedics, including knee and hip implants, surgical equipment, and neurovascular devices. Approximately 75 per cent of the company’s revenue is generated in the United States, with the remaining 25 per cent derived from international markets. Stryker is estimated to hold 75 per cent of the U.S. orthopedic surgical robotics market, providing a strong competitive position. Stryker is also well positioned to benefit from demographic trends, particularly an aging population and the associated increase in demand for joint replacements and surgical procedures. Stryker has a track record of dividend growth and offers a dividend yield of one per cent.

items._ogDesc: Russia and Ukraine on Tuesday held their first U.S.-mediated talks in nine months on ending their war, with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio calling the meeting “very productive” and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying the session was “constructive and quite substantive.”
items.body:
ABU DHABI, United Arab Emirates — Russia and Ukraine on Tuesday held their first U.S.-mediated talks in nine months on ending their war, with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio calling the meeting “very productive” and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying the session was “constructive and quite substantive.”

Hopes of ending Europe’s biggest conflict since World War II are tempered, however, by the absence of any significant breakthroughs in three previous rounds of talks earlier this year.

There’s nothing to suggest a new posture that would lead to a breakthrough, but circumstances surrounding the talks have been changed by the outcome of the U.S. midterm elections as well as increased pressure on Russia’s wartime economy. Moscow also is seeking to break Ukrainians’ will as winter sets in by ramping up its battering of the country’s power grid.

Neither Rubio nor Zelenskyy attended the talks in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates. The session lasted four hours and another is scheduled for a second day Wednesday.

Delegations from Moscow and Kyiv met as Washington, represented by U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and envoy Steve Witkoff, renewed its push to stop the fighting.

“It looks like the talks in Abu Dhabi were very productive,” Rubio said in Paris at the Group of Seven meeting, though he urged patience. “There’s a lot of work to be done in that regard. It’s not like something that’s on the verge of being solved in the next 24 hours or anything like that.”

Zelenskyy said the talks were largely about humanitarian issues, including prisoner exchanges and returning Ukrainian civilians in captivity, as well as children taken from the country. Security guarantees also were discussed, he added during an appearance at the University of Copenhagen in Denmark.

A senior Ukrainian official who spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorised to comment publicly said Ukraine and Russia talked about a large scale prisoner swap, although the details will be discussed in the coming days.

The 3-way meeting was the first since February

The two-day session is the first such meeting since February on the war, which analysts and humanitarian organizations say has killed hundreds of thousands of soldiers and thousands of civilians.

Kushner said he believed there were “some good ideas how to bridge” the differences between the two sides.

Trump, whose stance on the war has varied, must reckon with Democrats taking over the U.S. Congress in January following the U.S. elections. Democrats could demand more support for Ukraine.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told ZDF television on Monday night that “I don’t have overly high expectations” for the talks.

There are no signs the fighting is abating, and the talks come against a backdrop of new long-range strikes by both Russia and Ukraine. The two armies are largely deadlocked on the front line.

Russia launched 162 drones of various types and a ballistic missile at Ukraine overnight, Ukraine’s air force said.

Russia’s Defence Ministry said its forces downed 155 Ukrainian drones overnight in eight Russian regions, as well as over the Crimean Peninsula, which Moscow illegally annexed from Ukraine in 2014.

Kushner says the U.S. aims to build on past experience

Kushner said in opening remarks that the goal of the talks is to “create a new framework and a new understanding building upon the different institutions and understandings of the past.”

“We take what’s worked, we try to identify what’s failed, why we’re in this position and hopefully create a new framework that leads us for decades, if not centuries, of peace,” he said.

NATO commander U.S. Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, who was also present, said that the U.S. delegation looked forward “to working with both sides as we seek to advance the progress we’ve made in the past and continue this pursuit to set the foundations for a lasting peace.”

Rustem Umerov, the head of Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service who leads Kyiv’s delegation, thanked the U.S. for its efforts to end Russia’s invasion.

“Our people are waiting to end this war. And we hope that we will achieve the lasting peace for Ukraine,” he said.

Ukrainians meet first with European and NATO officials

The head of the Russian delegation, Vladimir Medinsky, expressed hope the meeting “will allow us to advance on the path towards peace in the interests of the people of Russia and the people of Ukraine.”

Umerov said the day began with a meeting between the Ukrainian team, the U.S. envoys and representatives from the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, NATO and the European Commission.

Russia has objected to the Europeans’ involvement in the three-way talks, but said EU representatives could join at a later stage.

Russia and Ukraine hold to their demands

The Russian and Ukrainian governments remain far apart on key elements of any prospective deal.

Russian President Vladimir Putin wants Ukraine to pull its troops back from four regions of Ukraine that Moscow annexed in September 2022 but has never fully captured. He also demands that Ukraine abandon its bid to join NATO and accept strict limits on its military, among other issues.

Putin wants a comprehensive peace deal on those conditions and won’t agree to a general halt in hostilities, arguing that it would only allow Ukrainian troops to rest and replenish their weapons stockpiles.

Zelenskyy rejects Putin’s demands to voluntarily cede territory. He also rejects any limits on Ukraine’s military or its arrangements with Western partners, which Kyiv sees as essential security guarantees to stop Moscow from invading again.

Ukraine argues an immediate ceasefire is the necessary first step toward negotiating a wider settlement and says a direct meeting between Putin and Zelenskyy is the only way territorial issues can be settled. Putin has spurned those suggestions.

Moscow and Kyiv sent experienced negotiators

The Russian and Ukrainian delegations include senior officials who have attended previous rounds of talks.

Russia’s chief negotiator is Medinsky, a Putin aide who has led Moscow’s team since the first full-fledged peace negotiations with Ukraine in Istanbul in March 2022, although exploratory talks took place earlier in neighboring Belarus. The Russian delegation also includes deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin and military intelligence chief Igor Kostyukov.

Besides Umerov, the Ukrainian delegation also reportedly includes Zelenskyy’s chief of staff, Kyrylo Budanov.

U.S. says a broader European security deal is in the works

Last week, Trump declared that some kind of grand deal about European security was in the works, describing it as “a big agreement” that is “going to involve more than Ukraine.”

Kushner said Monday on X that a “comprehensive and lasting settlement will also require direct engagement between Russia and our European partners on the broader security arrangements that affect them.”

Moscow has praised that approach.

John Leicester in Paris, Geir Moulson in Berlin, Susie Blann in Kyiv, Ukraine, and Barry Hatton in Lisbon, Portugal, contributed.

items._ogDesc: BMO sees Canada’s immigration changes doubling expected population growth in 2027, keeping housing demand higher as more temporary residents stay.
items.body:
Canada’s continuing its immigration experiments but this time it’s a little more discreet. Ottawa’s 2027-29 immigration plan maintains the current regular permanent resident admissions target. However, BMO notes that existing and new special measures mean the number of permanent residents will be much higher. As a result, the bank’s economists have nearly doubled their population growth forecast.

Canada’s Immigration Measures Lift Effective Target To 660,000

Ottawa’s immigration target may look conservative, but it’s much bigger than the fragmented announcements suggest. The 2027-2029 immigration plan maintains 380,000 admissions annually, but BMO projects the target is actually much higher than the headline numbers suggest.

“While Ottawa maintains permanent resident targets of 380k per year, special one-time measures (from both the 2025 and 2026 budgets) build significantly on that amount,” explains BMO senior economist Robert Kavcic.

Canada Hopes To Attract A Lot More Permanent Residents

Permanent residents: actual admissions, target admissions, and special measures.

Source: BMO Capital Markets; StatCan; Budget 2026.

He notes that special measures in Budget 2025 and 2026 add roughly 280,000 temporary-to-permanent resident transitions in 2027. “In other words, roughly 280k temporary residents will be granted permanent resident status in 2027, with officials suggesting this will be on top of new admissions,” says Kavcic. After the special measures, BMO puts the total closer to 660,000 permanent residents.

BMO Sees Population Growth Rebounding To Nearly 1% In 2027

The measures mean population growth is seen bouncing much higher than previously forecast. BMO now expects the population to expand roughly 1% in 2027, nearly double the 0.5% they previously anticipated. “In effect, because those temporary residents are now not leaving, they will not drag on population growth as previously expected,” explains Kavcic.

The special measures largely aim to keep people already in the country. Converting their status won’t immediately add housing demand, but fewer departures would mean fewer homes freed up for the temporary resident inflow. This reduced churn can boost housing demand more than previously anticipated, even without changing the headline immigration target.

“This is an abrupt change in the near-term outlook,” says Kavcic, questioning whether repeated one-time measures make planning harder for the Bank of Canada, homebuilders, and municipalities.

Since housing takes years to build, the read is that policymakers are trying to overshoot supply with further demand stimulus. However, the state of the Canadian economy is very different from last time it was attempted. With Canadians leaving in record volumes to find opportunities elsewhere, the ability to retain and attract immigrants may be harder than simply raising a quota.

items.title: What brokers need to know about an ever-evolving appraisal process
items.description: Appraisal executive emphasizes key differences in the alternative space
items.content: <p>Appraisal executive emphasizes key differences in the alternative space</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639299368595742752.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Appraisal executive emphasizes key differences in the alternative space
items.body:
Canadian mortgage brokers have established themselves as a key conduit between borrowers and lenders – but in the alternative lending space, that role expands to becoming the connector between borrower, lender, and appraiser.

That fact means it’s doubly important for brokers in the sector to take the time to understand what appraisers do and why they do it, according to Appraisal Institute of Canada (AIC) director Claudio Polito (pictured top). 

Among the main misconceptions about an appraiser’s role, Polito told Canadian Mortgage Professional, is that an appraisal is simply a property value. “To most people – the borrower, the broker, perhaps even the lender – the value is the most important part,” he said. “But to the appraiser, the value is just a component of it. There’s a story to be told.”

That story includes neighbourhood context, physical improvements, and market activity – all of which feed into the final opinion of value. Polito also pointed out that lender requirements vary considerably, and brokers should factor this into their preparation.

“Brokers are asked to know their client and we’re asking them to know their lender as well,” he said. “A Big Five bank may have one requirement. A private lending individual may have a different requirement. Even within the same space, there are different requirements.”

Polito’s main advice for brokers is on client preparation, an area he said too many brokers overlook until problems arise. His recommendation: get ahead of potential issues by asking the right questions early.

“Rather than having the appraiser highlight potential areas of concern, have the broker be made aware of that first,” he said. “Do you have a basement apartment? Is it registered? Is it approved by the municipality? Do you have an addition? Was it done with or without permits? These are questions the appraiser will ask – better we know up front.”

What’s changed in the current market

In the current climate, expectation management on value is equally important – especially because of the significant drop in values across many markets since the peak of 2021 and 2022. The borrowers who purchased at the height of the market sometimes carry expectations that no longer reflect reality, according to Polito.

“If you purchased your property in Toronto in 2022 for $1 million and you’re asking for a home line of credit and thinking the property is worth $1.5 million, what makes you think the property has gone up half a million dollars when everything in the news says the Toronto market is declining?” he said.

The condo market has suffered an especially noteworthy downturn, leading to appraisal challenges as buyers who purchased preconstruction units are suddenly unable to secure a mortgage for the amount they agreed to buy the property for years back.

How AI is impacting the appraisal process

Another big trend to impact the appraisals space in recent years, unsurprisingly, has been artificial intelligence (AI). The rise of AI-driven property valuations is having a big say on how some borrowers, and even some lenders, approach the question of what a property is worth.

Polito still believes AI will never completely eradicate the human influence from the appraisal process. “AI can be a great tool when it’s properly applied with guardrails in place, when there’s the human element and the human involvement in it,” he said.

“But you’re seeing more and more homeowners and borrowers relying on AI – and that could be dangerous. It could lead to false expectations, either overstated or understated.”

On automated valuation models (AVMs), increasingly used by lenders in lower-risk transactions, Polito is also sceptical whether their influence will ultimately threaten the human factor.

“Take those with a grain of salt, knowing that what a platform spits out may not be completely accurate in the same way that what a professional appraiser might conclude the property is worth,” he said.

“An appraiser uses all of their senses as part of the analysis. An appraiser sees what the analytical computer doesn’t see.”

items.title: National Bank acquires Embark in $226M education savings deal
items.description: The deal brings 436,000 RESP beneficiaries under National Bank’s wealth management umbrella
items.content: <p>The deal brings 436,000 RESP beneficiaries under National Bank’s wealth management umbrella</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639299339464127761.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: The deal brings 436,000 RESP beneficiaries under National Bank’s wealth management umbrella
items.body:
National Bank of Canada has agreed to acquire Embark Student Corp. for approximately $226 million, gaining a digitally driven national education savings platform and more than $6 billion in assets under management.

The deal brings National Bank roughly 436,000 Registered Education Savings Plan (RESP) beneficiaries managed through Embark’s tech-enabled platform, with closing expected by mid-fiscal 2027, subject to court and regulatory approvals.

The transaction extends National Bank’s retail banking reach into Ontario and Western Canada — markets where the Montreal-headquartered lender has pursued a series of strategic acquisitions, including its 2024 agreement to acquire Canadian Western Bank.

For Canadian mortgage brokers, the deal signals a wider industry shift: the country’s major banks are competing not just on rates but on the depth of integrated family financial planning they can offer — from housing debt to education savings to retirement.

“We are happy to see Embark joining National Bank,” said Nancy Paquet, Executive Vice-President, Wealth Management at National Bank of Canada.

“This transaction is strongly aligned with our savings and investment advisory strategy for our clients, combining Embark’s digital capabilities with National Bank’s strengths to deliver a best-in-class education savings experience and expand our presence across Canada. We look forward to welcoming Embark’s employees and clients in the next months.”

Read more: RBC to acquire Australian fund manager Yarra Capital in 2027 deal

A platform built for record RESP adoption

The acquisition arrives as Canadian families turn to RESPs in growing numbers.

Statistics Canada’s 2025 Survey of Approaches to Educational Planning, released February 20, found that 89% of children with dedicated education savings held an RESP that year, up from 85% in 2020.

At the same time, financial anxiety now grips roughly 60% of Canadians, making education savings an increasingly contested priority in household budgets that brokers are helping clients navigate day to day.

“Joining forces with National Bank accelerates our mission to make education savings accessible to every Canadian parent,” said Andrew Lo, CEO and President of Embark Student Corp.

“This partnership reflects a shared commitment to that goal, and it’s why this is the right fit at the right time. We are excited to continue delivering best-in-class RESP services and advice, now alongside National Bank.”

Read more: Tru Cooperative Bank broadens its broker reach across Canada

Transaction structure and what clients can expect

The deal will be implemented by way of a plan of arrangement under the Canada Business Corporations Act and requires approval from the Ontario Superior Court of Justice.

National Bank’s Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) ratio is expected to decline by approximately 10 basis points on closing.

The acquisition price of approximately $226 million is subject to working capital adjustments.

Embark customers will see no immediate changes. Daily operations, government grant applications, and RESP investment management all continue as normal.

Founded in 1859 and headquartered in Montreal, Québec, National Bank of Canada is one of Canada’s six systemically important banks. It reported a 23% rise in third-quarter 2026 net income and held approximately $635 billion in assets as at July 31. 

The company employs roughly 37,000 people across its five business segments: Personal Banking, Commercial Banking, Wealth Management, Capital Markets, and ABA Bank. 

Embark Student Corp., meanwhile, is Canada’s digital education savings and planning company, headquartered in Toronto. It manages RESPs for approximately 436,000 beneficiaries nationwide and holds more than $6 billion in assets under management.

Registered as a Scholarship Plan Dealer across Canada, Embark provides end-to-end investment management, government grant administration, and digital savings tools to Canadian families.

It operates as a wholly owned subsidiary of Embark Student Foundation, a not-for-profit Canadian corporation that serves as the current promoter of the Embark plans.

items.title: How Canada’s mortgage market has handled the renewal wave
items.description: Lending executive on whether talk of a renewal ‘cliff’ was overblown
items.content: <p>Lending executive on whether talk of a renewal ‘cliff’ was overblown</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0343_639299340826703449.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Lending executive on whether talk of a renewal ‘cliff’ was overblown
items.body:
At MortgageFest Canada, we caught up with Grant Armstrong, chief growth officer at WealthOne Bank of Canada, to hear what lenders are discussing with brokers – and why the mortgage market to date has been able to withstand the wave of renewals some feared could cause significant challenges for the market.

[00:00] We had a road map at the beginning of the year of tools that would take about two to three years to get done. We got them all done last month. How many brokers in here are doing TikToks and they're actually seeing a benefit from it? I think everyone got really worried about it so they got really good at preparing for it. The renewal cliff doesn't exist to the extreme. We're not going to just talk about mortgages. We're going to talk about everything.

[00:32] Fergal McAlinden: Now, so we are back with Grant Armstrong, Chief Growth Officer at Wealth One Bank of Canada. As we were saying, Grant, really busy start to the year for everybody. It's been a, well, not start to the year, it's been an interesting year for everyone. Talk about your message to brokers today. There are plenty of them here. What are you guys talking about?

[00:51] Grant Armstrong: Yeah, the biggest thing we're trying to do is explain to brokers who we are. Wealth One Bank is actually Canada's fastest growing bank. So what we want to be able to do is understand what our message is, what we're focusing on, our goals, how we can help the industry, how we can partner with brokers better, but also just why we're different.

[01:08] I mean, it's incredible. The number of organizations that are here today. I do remember the very first event about four years ago and it would fit maybe two rows. You've sold out an incredible location here. So, we want to tell people why we're different, why we believe in them, what we're trying to help them with, and go forward from there.

[01:26] Fergal McAlinden: It always strikes me that for events like this, one of the biggest advantages for both brokers and lenders is that you get a chance to talk to each other about maybe some of the pain points, things that are going well, things that are going badly. Is there anything that you commonly see with brokers or agents that you think you'd like to get the message out that needs to be different or that maybe they're not doing that they should be doing at the moment?

[01:45] Grant Armstrong: Yeah, I think this is a great opportunity to sit down with brokers and talk to them about what they're doing, but we're doing it a little differently. We're trying to understand what their pain points are. And the biggest pain points that we're hearing from brokers is the ever-changing policies, the ever-changing rules, the ever-changing processes that lenders are introducing.

[02:03] Every lender in the room is just trying to be more efficient, more productive. So every single week a lender has changed how you submit a deal, what forms you need, what documents. Brokers are struggling to keep up with that information. So what we're trying to do is actually, we did all of our changes earlier this year and we're actually trying to tell everyone we're status quo.

[02:23] All the changes that we're doing are back-end changes, but they get to see the benefit. So we brought in AI, for example. We're using AI to build tools. We had a road map at the beginning of the year of tools that would take about two to three years to get done, and we got them all done last month.

[02:38] So that's what we're doing on the back end. We want to hear what their pain points are, make sure they know that we're changing what we do in the back, but it's not impacting them except for all the positive sides of that.

[02:48] The other part is we're trying to get people to understand the credit environment. Between regulators, between people south of the border, between wars, it all impacts mortgage interest rates, it all impacts process, it all impacts risk. So how, as a lender, as a Schedule I bank, are we interpreting that and how are we putting it back out there? Those are the conversations we're having.

[03:12] Fergal McAlinden: It's interesting you mention that. You and I have been talking over the years, probably starting around COVID time. We had record low interest rates, we had economic turmoil, all that. Then we moved into rate spikes. There was talk about the renewal cliff and all that kind of thing. Then we have all the geopolitical tensions that we've seen over the past couple of years, condo challenges and more.

[03:32] What about the market for 2026? How are you viewing it? And anything you're keeping in mind navigating the current outlook?

[03:38] Grant Armstrong: I'm going to sound like a broken record. I've been saying this for four years. The markets are good. And what I love about what brokers have done is they've diversified.

[03:47] A lot of people say, "Oh, the market's slow." No. Purchase transactions are slow in some areas, but refinancing, switching, consolidating, improvements, investor opportunities, there are brokers I was talking to the other day that have paired up with wealth management organizations to be able to help people fund investments and fund savings.

[04:04] So the diversity of what brokers are doing has kind of negated the market trends. Ten or fifteen years ago you could see seasonality. That's gone. It's now an opportunity that sits 60, 90, 120 days in front of you. So lenders that can actually adapt to that change and keep their processes, policies, and marketing top of mind are benefiting from that.

[04:28] The other conversation I had a long chat about yesterday was brokers getting much more into marketing. It used to be business groups, handshakes, and realtors. But social media. I mean, how many brokers in here are doing TikToks and they're actually seeing a benefit from it?

[04:43] So, I think 2026 is going to end on a high. Not to dampen the market, I think rates will probably go up in October. I think the governor basically alluded to that without alluding to it the other day. We'll see shifts.

[04:56] But what you can also see on the fixed-rate side of the market is they've already been going up. GIC rates are up 35 points in the last 60 to 90 days. Bond rates are up 60 points. Everything's been going up already. It's just a natural part of the market.

[05:12] Fergal McAlinden: What about when it comes to the renewal? We've talked about that so much over the past few years. We were all looking to the cliff that we talked about in 2025 and 2026. Do you get the impression that it's been more manageable than we maybe thought a couple of years back, or what's your look on that one?

[05:26] Grant Armstrong: I think it was a war cry. I think what it was is, we're going to anchor around this. The reality is 20% to 40% of mortgages renew every two years. That's just the reality. Shorter terms have driven that number up.

[05:40] I think everyone got really worried about it, so they got really good at preparing for it. And I think that preparation has taken the noise out of it. The big renewal cliff was in 2021 when rates were around 1.99% to 2.49% and then in a year or two they were renewing at 6% to 7%.

[05:58] That was the renewal cliff. That happened to alternative lenders, private lenders, and others. But prime lenders took three- and five-year terms. They skipped it. So they were able to start renewing again as rates started to come down.

[06:10] We're in normal rates today. We're not in obscenely high rates. We're in normal rates. So I think the renewal cliff doesn't exist to the extreme, but it's something we need to be aware of.

[06:21] And the stress test, as much as many people don't love it, worked. Every customer was qualified at at least 5.25%. Rates are below 5.25%, so they should be able to handle it.

[06:32] Fergal McAlinden: Yeah. The stress test, I feel, is always the one regulatory thing that a lot of brokers pointed to and said this should go or it served its purpose. But its purpose was to do what it did, I guess, and it really helped.

[06:45] Grant Armstrong: It's a barrier, don't get me wrong. The stress test does limit some deals, but it's necessary. It constrained people from going out too far. Some of those customers that didn't have a stress test, when rates were 1.99%, would be getting three- and four-million-dollar mortgages. They'd be in a lot of trouble now. So it's a necessary tool that was required.

[07:05] Fergal McAlinden: Sure. Okay, so Wealth One. Anything that you're really excited to share today? Anything coming down the line that we should be keeping an eye on?

[07:12] Grant Armstrong: Wealth One is advancing beyond just being a mortgage lender. Last week we actually did a massive campaign in Toronto. We're helping Canadians save. We have Canada's highest-rate non-promotional savings account. We're helping Canadians on both sides of that balance sheet.

[07:28] I don't want to give too much away, but we've got a few more enhancements on those products. We also want to see how we can help brokers be much more involved in that. I think brokers have this incredible opportunity to sit in front of customers.

[07:41] It started with mortgages. Creditor insurance came out a couple of years after that, and it hasn't really crossed into other product lines. I want to see how we can actually position brokers as that adviser to the customer and give them more tools, more products in front of them.

[07:55] So we have a number of changes that are going to amplify our business on both sides of the balance sheet, but we want to be able to have that conversation with brokers about both sides. That's the big change you're going to see with us. We're not going to just talk about mortgages. We're going to talk about everything and really make sure that brokers are advised on everything they need to give customers.

[08:10] Fergal McAlinden: Okay, perfect. Last question, Grant, before I let you go. You've been at a few of these events. You were here when it was the Mortgage Summit. Now we're at Mortgage Fest. What's your impression of the event so far?

[08:19] Grant Armstrong: Oh, it's incredible. I was talking to somebody. Four years ago, when you planned it, there were maybe 230 people that might make it, and it was almost a thousand. This is a must-see event.

[08:33] If you're a broker and you want to talk to lenders, you want to talk to other people, you want to hear great speakers, you want to get insights, this is the place you need to be. And as a lender, I wouldn't be anywhere else.

[08:45] I congratulate you guys and the team. You had a mission four years ago. You gave me an opportunity to be part of that four years ago. I was on stage at your first one. I'm happy to look forward to the next 10 or 20 that you do and be there and support each one of them.

[09:01] Fergal McAlinden: Great stuff. Well, we're looking forward to seeing what's next from you guys from Wealth One and seeing what's in store for the rest of the year. So, thank you very much.

[09:08] Grant Armstrong: Thanks, guys.

items.description: CMI Financial’s Kevin Fettig says new financing rules need matching action on zoning and approvals
items.content: <p>CMI Financial’s Kevin Fettig says new financing rules need matching action on zoning and approvals</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639299329091481602.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: CMI Financial’s Kevin Fettig says new financing rules need matching action on zoning and approvals
items.body:
Canada’s 2026 federal budget delivered the most ambitious set of housing finance reforms in a generation — but Kevin Fettig (pictured top), president of CMI Financial Group in Toronto, says the policies won’t translate into housing supply without faster, coordinated action from municipalities on zoning and approvals.

Tabled by the Carney government on November 5, Budget 2026 commits $45 billion to the Build Canada Homes (BCH) initiative.

The package expands construction loan-to-value ratios to 90% for triplexes and fourplexes from February 1, 2027, allows private insurers to compete with the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) on five-to-50-unit properties, and raises the optional insurance cap to $1.5 million for buyers with a 20% deposit in some of Canada’s most competitive markets.

Fettig welcomed the direction while cautioning against optimism outpacing execution.

“There’s promise here, especially for smaller developers who have struggled to access capital,” he told Canadian Mortgage Professional.

“But beyond financing, municipal approvals, zoning restrictions, and the availability of construction funding are all crucial to help move things forward. The government needs to make sure these policies work together to help revitalize a struggling real estate market.”

Missing middle financing needs zoning to follow

The 90% loan-to-value threshold for small multi-unit homes — the triplexes, fourplexes, and low-rise rentals that form the backbone of “missing middle” housing — opens financing options that have long been beyond reach for smaller builders in markets where municipal approval delays stretch two to three years or more.

“For smaller builders, access to construction loans of up to 90 per cent of projected completion value, without property value caps, could make more triplexes, fourplexes and low-rise rental projects viable,” Fettig noted.

“Municipalities now need to streamline zoning and approvals so builders can put that financing to work instead of waiting years to get started.”

The federal government has proposed an extension of the ban on non-resident foreign homebuyers for a further two years, but says it would exclude new residential properties from the policy. https://t.co/6KdPDC1AMh — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 9, 2026

What the budget means for brokers

Fettig flagged the proposed Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) income verification pilot — a three-year, $13-million initiative set to begin testing in 2027-28 — as a fraud-prevention measure the broker industry has pressed Ottawa to deliver for years.

“The proposed CRA mortgage income verification service is long overdue, and it could give lenders another tool to detect fraud,” he said.

“For lenders like CMI, reliable income verification makes underwriting stronger.”

CMI has separately advocated for CMHC to introduce a mortgage-backed securities (MBS) pool to securitize insured construction loans, a move Fettig says would open a critical new funding channel for developers.

On insured mortgage rate transparency, Fettig underlined the broker’s irreplaceable role. 

“A low rate is only part of the picture, particularly when insurance premiums are added to the mortgage and repaid with interest, prepayment penalties vary from lender-to-lender and upfront incentives can be clawed back on an early payout,” he explained.

“That’s where brokers come in, helping borrowers understand the full cost of a mortgage and choose one that fits their needs.”

items.title: Bank of Canada survey points to higher rates and yields through 2028
items.description: Market participants see rates and bond yields rising, with risks skewed firmly upward
items.content: <p>Market participants see rates and bond yields rising, with risks skewed firmly upward</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639299291949382844.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Market participants see rates and bond yields rising, with risks skewed firmly upward
items.body:
Financial market participants have revised their interest rate and bond yield forecasts upward, with the median five-year Government of Canada bond yield climbing 35 basis points quarter-over-quarter to 3.50%, the Bank of Canada reported.

For Canadian mortgage brokers advising fixed-rate clients, the numbers signal continued pressure on long-term borrowing costs well into 2027.

The Bank of Canada’s third-quarter Market Participants Survey, conducted September 23 to October 1 among approximately 25 financial market professionals, recorded an identical 35-basis-point rise in the 2027 five-year bond yield forecast, to 3.45%.

Since five-year Government of Canada bond yields serve as the primary benchmark for fixed mortgage pricing, the upward revision carries direct renewal implications for brokers and their clients alike.

Rate risks tilt decisively upward

The survey reveals a sharp recalibration in market risk sentiment. Some 52% of respondents now view risks to their policy rate forecasts as skewed toward a higher path, up from 40% in Q2 2026.

Zero respondents see risk tilted toward lower rates, a reversal from 28% who held that view the previous quarter, and the clearest signal yet that markets have abandoned expectations of further relief.

The median policy rate forecast for December rose to 2.50% from 2.25%, with the consensus terminal rate settling at 2.75% from March 2027 through end-2028.

The Bank of Canada’s October 28 rate hike to 2.50%, which occurred after the survey window closed, aligned the actual rate with the December projection.

The median year-end 2026 Consumer Price Index (CPI) forecast also rose, to 3.0% from 2.6%, while GDP growth is projected at 1.6% for 2026 and 1.8% for 2027.

Canada’s labour market shed 4,700 jobs in October, pushing the national unemployment rate to 6.7% from 6.5%, a third consecutive month of deterioration that is now complicating the Bank of Canada’s (BoC) path to a December rate hike. https://t.co/dptjDonezZ — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 6, 2026

What brokers should tell renewal clients now

Marc Ercolao, economist at TD Economics in Toronto, previously said that the October hike was designed to buy time.

“We think this hike buys the Bank a few months to assess whether higher energy and input costs are actually filtering through to consumer prices,” he said, projecting one further 25-basis-point increase in Q1-2027.

CIBC economist Andrew Grantham projected a December hold but sees the terminal rate at 2.75% all the same.

“We don’t expect that core measures of inflation will accelerate as much as the Bank fears, which should become more obvious early in 2027 and allow the Bank of Canada to then hold interest rates at 2.75% throughout the remainder of next year,” he said.

Joel Fox, chief operating officer of Ownright, a Toronto-based digital real estate law platform, stressed the need for proactive client conversations.

“If you’re renewing in the next year, start early. It’s a good idea to talk to your lender or broker, compare offers and know what your payment will be before the renewal notice shows up,” Fox explained.

items.title: Real estate association forecasts B.C. home sales to slide 4.5 per cent this year
items.description: VANCOUVER — The B.C. Real Estate Association expects home sales in the province to continue to slide this year, warning of "mounting headwinds" for the market, while hoping for a pick-up in both prices and sales in 2027.
items._ogDesc: VANCOUVER — The B.C. Real Estate Association expects home sales in the province to continue to slide this year, warning of "mounting headwinds" for the market, while hoping for a pick-up in both prices and sales in 2027.
items.body:
VANCOUVER — The B.C. Real Estate Association expects home sales in the province to continue to slide this year, warning of "mounting headwinds" for the market, while hoping for a pick-up in both prices and sales in 2027.

The association says in its fourth-quarter forecast that sales are expected to fall 4.5 per cent this year from 2025 levels, to just over 67,000 units sold.

Association chief economist Brendon Ogmundson says in a statement that prospective buyers this year had several reasons to hesitate, including an oil-price shock, trade tensions with the United States, slower immigration and rising interest rates.

The forecast says active listings in B.C. are at their highest levels since 2015, and new-home inventory is also elevated.

It predicts that the supply pressure will push the average home price down 1.2 per cent to just over $941,000.

The forecast calls for a "modest recovery" in 2027 with sales projected to increase 7.2 per cent, but Ogmundson says that's in anticipation of a decline in the impacts of new U.S. tariffs and reductions in fixed mortgage rates.

"Hopefully, a calming of these headwinds next year should stimulate housing activity, which, paired with flattening inventories, is expected to drive price growth of 2.4 per cent in 2027, bringing the provincial average price to $964,200," the forecast says, adding it is anticipating a "long-awaited rebound" in the Lower Mainland market.

Greater Vancouver home sales are projected to reach 23,000 units this year, down 3 per cent from the year before, while the Fraser Valley is forecast to see a 4.4 per cent decrease to 11,000 units.

The largest decline is expected in the Chilliwack area of the Lower Mainland, with unit sales falling from 2,300 last year to 1,900 this year, an 18-per-cent decrease.

"Following a 2025 that saw the weakest year of sales in over a decade, faint signs of a 2026 recovery were thwarted by a resurgent oil price shock and further escalation in Canada’s trade war with the United States," the forecast says.

"With population growth expected to remain subdued through 2027, B.C. faces limited capacity to grow at trend levels."

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 10, 2026.

items.title: Applications Open For New Program Levelling Up Canada’s Project Leaders
items.description:
Canada’s push to build is well underway, and the major projects now being planned and delivered need people truly prepared to lead them.

For many organizations, those people are already on the team, bringing with them 10 to 15 years of experience, a strong track record running projects, and the ambition to take the next step.

Now, a new program is poised to prepare those leaders. The Canadian Infrastructure Leadership Academy, launched by the University of Toronto’s Infrastructure Institute at the School of Cities and the Rotman School of Management, is the only executive program built specifically for major project leaders in Canada. Applications are now open, and are being reviewed on a rolling basis.

The academy offers what neither an MBA nor a project management certification does: a specialized focus on major-project leadership, from building teams across the many organizations that share a major project to negotiating the conflict that so often arises. Developed in collaboration with industry and government leaders, the program brings public and private sector participants together, so each cohort leaves with a national network of senior peers.

Over six months, the hybrid program combines three three-day in-person modules at Rotman in Toronto with monthly live online sessions, mentorship and a capstone project. Participants work through a real issue from their own professional contexts with mentor support, so the value builds as the program progresses. Graduates earn a certificate from the Rotman School of Management.

For leaders outside Ontario, the in-person portion comes down to three three-day modules, with the rest of the program delivered online. The academy is designed to grow into a national program, delivered locally across the country. The first cohort, launching April 13, 2027, will bring together an intentionally diverse group of leaders from civil infrastructure, energy, natural resources, and industrial projects, so a participant from Calgary or Vancouver leaves with connections well beyond their own market.

“A lot is being staked right now on being able to build big things,” says Matti Siemiatycki, Academic Co-Director at the Canadian Infrastructure Leadership Academy. The projects themselves have grown more complex, too. In Siemiatycki’s words, today’s major project is “an IT project wrapped in steel,” involving ever more parties, and ever more technology.

That pressure is especially visible out West. Insights from Altus Group’s 2026 Canadian Cost Guide found overall construction costs in Calgary and Edmonton rose 4% or more year over year, even as they fell in Toronto and Vancouver. Further, BuildForce Canada projects that 43,700 of Alberta’s construction workers — or, about 21% of the province’s 2025 construction labour force — will retire by 2035, just as non-residential construction is expected to grow. All the while, the Canadian Construction Association’s summer 2026 economic report points to growing use of sector-specific tariffs and local procurement measures, along with the domestic requirements that come with them.

These aren’t easy conditions, but they’re exactly the conditions the curriculum is built for. Alongside leadership and negotiation, participants work on commercial leadership, procurement, and governance, as well as the behavioural biases that lead projects to underestimate costs, all skills that matter more when budgets are under pressure and experienced people are leaving the industry.

For the companies delivering those projects, much of that complexity turns into risk. The way today’s contracts are written, Siemiatycki says, companies take on a huge amount of it — especially in construction — and when a project goes badly, they absorb the cost. That makes training the people in charge a strategic business decision. Giving leaders the most modern techniques to guide projects of this nature, he says, “is a risk mitigation strategy.” With tuition priced in line with comparable academies in the UK and Australia, it’s an investment in the people carrying that risk.

For organizations deciding who will lead their next major project, the inaugural cohort is a chance to prepare that person now. Leaders can apply directly, and organizations can nominate a member of their team to apply.

Spots are limited. Apply by November 30th to secure a 20% discount.
