The post Canada To Add 200,000 Permanent Resident Spots, Housing Boost Limited appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: Canada’s Budget 2026 adds 200,000 permanent resident spots in 2027, but the housing demand boost is limited as recipients already live here.
items.body:
Canada is adjusting its immigration plan after a recent slowdown in population growth. Budget 2026 shows the country is adding 200,000 permanent resident spots in 2027. On top of regular admissions and existing programs, the total can exceed 580,000 spots by the end of next year. However, this won’t add much to housing demand, as the extra spaces aim to retain people already here and reduce population churn.

Canadian Immigration Targets Vs Reality

Before diving into the changes, let’s clarify that immigration targets aren’t hard numbers. Ottawa isn’t just making a DoorDash order for 10,000 Guinean students; it sets a target. Meeting that target depends on global demand, domestic processing, and applicant follow-through.

IRCC data shows only 216,600 regular permanent resident admissions in the first 8 months of 2026. That’s just 57% of the target with only a third of the year left, making that a tough goal to hit. Canadian taxpayers actually spent millions to create that post-pandemic study permit surge. Ottawa’s caps only appeared after applications cratered, as qualified demand was exhausted. But don’t let that ruin the narrative of unlimited growth that policymakers want you to believe.

It’s important to understand that immigration targets are similar to a public company’s earnings projections, but instead of boosting a stock price, they bolster Canada’s projected economic growth and access to debt. Whether global demand is there to fulfil the targets remains to be seen. Now let’s move on to the changes.

Canada Trims Temporary Arrivals, Adds 200k Permanent Resident Spots

Budget 2026 reveals fewer new temporary arrivals and more permanent spots. The 2027 immigration targets maintain 380,000 regular permanent admissions and 370,000 new temporary arrivals annually through 2029. That’s a 3.9% reduction (15,000 spots) in new temporary arrivals from the 2026 target, as previously announced. The big change is additional targeted permanent resident spots.

Canada plans to add up to 200,000 permanent resident spots in 2027, up to 100,000 for workers and their families, and up to 100,000 for specified humanitarian and family applicants. Combined with the existing target, it lifts potential permanent resident admissions to 580,000, 52.6% higher than the regular admission target. That’s on top of the earlier initiatives that targeted the transition of 148,000 temporary to permanent residents in 2026-27. Admissions could exceed 580,000 with those earlier initiatives.

Interestingly, it’s accompanied by a reduction to the Federal High Skilled admissions program, which will fall from the previously planned target of 111,000 people to 100,000. However, provincial nominee admissions will rise by 2,500 to 95,000, while the Atlantic Immigration Program rises from 4,000 to 6,000 targeted admissions. Rather than an outright reduction, it looks like Ottawa is hoping to better target regional growth.

More Permanent Residents Don’t Mean More Population Growth

The addition of 200,000 permanent residents won’t directly add to aggregate demand, especially housing. These admissions will only shift people from temporary residents to permanent ones, so their consumption is already reflected today. This distinction was also made clear by the PBO earlier this year, when they reported 48% of permanent residents in 2025 were previously international students or temporary workers.

As we explained earlier this year, Ottawa promised to reduce non-permanent residents as a share of the population, but was initially light on the details. Part of that plan is to turn temporary residents into permanent ones, which the PBO found necessary under the previous plan to hit the target of below 5% by the end of 2027, a delay of a year. Budget 2026 appears to be buying policymakers some more room to help them hit that target.

items.title: Here are the 7 luxury markets outperforming Toronto and Vancouver
items.description: REMAX Canada finds five markets posting double-digit gains as larger urban centres pull back
items.content: <p>REMAX Canada finds five markets posting double-digit gains as larger urban centres pull back</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0321_638175884653377179.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: REMAX Canada finds five markets posting double-digit gains as larger urban centres pull back
items.body:
Seven of 13 Canadian luxury housing markets recorded year-over-year sales increases in the nine months to September 30, with five posting double-digit gains, even as Greater Vancouver and the Greater Toronto Area (GTA) retreated sharply, according to REMAX Canada’s Fall/Winter 2026 Spotlight on Luxury Report.

Burlington led national luxury growth at 26.3%, followed by St. John’s, Newfoundland and Labrador (+21%), Calgary (+20.6%), Edmonton (+15.9%), and Saskatoon (+15.3%).

Ottawa (+7.6%) and Winnipeg (+3%) also posted gains.

Greater Vancouver fell 17%, Oakville 16.7%, and the GTA 9.4% at their respective luxury thresholds, a divergence the publication has tracked since Canada’s sharpest housing market split in years became visible in first-quarter data.

Don Kottick, President of REMAX Canada, said conventional market variables are no longer the whole story.

“Regional economic strength is shaping luxury demand, with stronger economies providing a sturdier foundation for homebuying activity,” Kottick said.

“Traditional drivers such as supply and demand, pricing, purchasing power and interest rates alone are no longer the only reliable predictors of market activity. Market dynamics are evolving, becoming more complex and nuanced, and increasingly dependent on regional fundamentals.”

What’s driving gains in smaller markets

The theme is consistent with what CMP reported in June, when tracking why luxury buyers are leaving major markets for smaller cities had shifted from a cyclical question to a structural one.

“Smaller and mid-sized markets are experiencing increasing or stable conditions at the higher end of the luxury segment, largely supported by economic diversification, population growth, and continued demand for lifestyle-oriented properties,” Kottick told CMP at the time.

“Meanwhile, in the country’s largest and more expensive markets, uncertainty has prompted affluent buyers to take a more measured approach.”

Ultra-luxury holds above the declines

Despite headline drops in Toronto and Vancouver, the top of the market proved more durable.

GTA sales above $7.5 million climbed 17.6% year over year, with 15 transactions exceeding $10 million in the City of Toronto, the highest tally in a decade.

Oakville sales above $5 million rose close to 18%, even as overall luxury sales above $3.25 million fell 16.7%.

Greater Vancouver’s detached market above $5 million declined 8%, significantly less than the 17% drop in the broader segment above $3 million.

A development since the study period closed also bears watching: the Bank of Canada raised its policy rate by 25 basis points to 2.5% on October 28, adding a fresh financing variable for buyers dependent on mortgages or the sale of an existing home.

Michael Altneu, Vice President of Luxury at REMAX Canada, said buyer readiness is not in question. Confidence is.

“Wealth enables a home purchase; confidence and the right opportunity motivate it,” Altneu said.

“Most luxury buyers have the financial resources to act, but economic and geopolitical concerns are giving purchasers reason to pause. That said, a property that meets their every expectation can still spur a buyer, especially given the narrower price gap between existing homes and move-up properties, particularly in smaller markets.”

That narrowing gap, a pattern consistent with how secondary luxury markets are outshining Toronto and Vancouver in sales velocity, also drove some of the report’s most notable transactions: a $28-million waterfront estate in Vancouver, a Forest Hill home in Toronto that sold for more than $23 million, and an $18.5-million waterfront property in Oakville.

items.description: Canada’s largest bank eyes Asia-Pacific growth with Melbourne-based fund manager deal
items.content: <p>Canada’s largest bank eyes Asia-Pacific growth with Melbourne-based fund manager deal</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639298482233952768.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Canada’s largest bank eyes Asia-Pacific growth with Melbourne-based fund manager deal
items.body:
Royal Bank of Canada (RBC) has agreed to acquire Yarra Capital Management Limited, an independent Australian fund manager overseeing approximately A$18 billion in assets as at September 30.

The deal places Canada’s largest bank firmly on the Asia-Pacific map and signals an increasingly global strategy for one of the country’s most dominant financial institutions.

The agreement is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027, pending satisfaction of certain conditions including regulatory approval from Australian authorities.

RBC confirmed the transaction will not significantly affect its common equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital ratio — the standard measure of a bank’s financial buffer under international banking rules — or its future run-rate earnings.

Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed.

A springboard for global asset management

Founded in 1864 and listed on both the Toronto Stock Exchange and the New York Stock Exchange, Royal Bank of Canada is Canada’s largest bank by market capitalisation.

Its asset management arm, RBC Global Asset Management (RBC GAM), oversaw approximately $1.70 trillion in assets as at July 31, with the bank’s wealth management segment delivering total revenue of CA$6.41 billion in the fiscal third quarter of 2026, up 16% year over year.

RBC GAM is a provider of global investment management services and solutions to institutional, high-net-worth and individual investors through separate accounts, pooled funds, mutual funds, hedge funds, exchange-traded funds and specialty investment strategies.

The acquisition follows earlier international moves by RBC GAM, including the purchase of London-based fixed income specialist BlueBay Asset Management, and extends a deliberate push to build market share outside North America. 

"The investment and distribution capabilities of Yarra are complementary to our asset management business. Yarra’s reputation within Australian fixed income and equities is a testament to its strong track record in investment performance and culture of putting clients first," said Damon Williams, chief executive officer of RBC GAM in Toronto.

 "We know Australian institutional investors and intermediaries take a globally oriented approach to asset allocation. We believe the strength of our investment capabilities that go beyond domestic borders within fixed income, equities and alternatives are well-positioned to support this investor appetite."

An independent Australian firm with Asia-Pacific reach

Founded in 2017, Yarra Capital Management operates from offices in Melbourne and Sydney.

The firm specialises in Australian fixed income, equities, and alternative investment solutions, with access to international equity strategies through third-party manager partnerships.

Yarra serves the Australian institutional and retail markets, and its Australian investment products are accessed from various international markets, including Japan and New Zealand. 

Dion Hershan, executive chairman of Yarra Capital Management in Melbourne, described the agreement as the result of a thorough and deliberate search:

“After a long and deliberate search to find the right business partner for the future, we are thrilled about our agreement to join RBC. The strong cultural alignment between Yarra and RBC is very clear and we share the same fundamental beliefs of serving our clients with compelling products and services, delivering investment excellence and developing and retaining the best talent.”

For Canadian mortgage professionals tracking where the Big Six are directing capital, the acquisition points unmistakably outward.

Marcos De Souza, a banking analyst at Morningstar DBRS in Toronto, told Canadian Mortgage Professional in December 2025 that domestic consolidation options were fast narrowing.

“The Canadian market is so small,” De Souza said. “There’s not much further merger and acquisition space in 2026 in the Canadian sense. I don’t know where it would come from.”

With the Yarra deal, RBC has found its answer across the Pacific.

items.title: FSRA issues conditions on Ontario agent over unpaid 2018 penalty
items.description: Agent settles with FSRA, agreeing to pay a $30,000 penalty outstanding since 2018
items.content: <p>Agent settles with FSRA, agreeing to pay a $30,000 penalty outstanding since 2018</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639298474539637558.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Agent settles with FSRA, agreeing to pay a $30,000 penalty outstanding since 2018
items.body:
The Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Ontario (FSRA) has imposed conditions on the insurance agent licence of Victor Ferreira following a settlement over administrative penalties that went unpaid for more than six years.

Ferreira and his company, Ferreira Insurance and Investment Concepts Inc. (FIIC), failed to pay administrative monetary penalties (AMPs) of $30,000 and $45,000 respectively, both imposed in April 2018 for conduct contrary to the Mortgage Brokerages, Lenders and Administrators Act, 2006 (MBLAA).

Despite invoices issued by the Ontario Minister of Finance in September 2019, neither sum was paid.

FIIC has since withdrawn its insurance agent licence renewal application.

A decade of deferred consequences

Ferreira had also held a mortgage agent licence under the MBLAA from August 25, 2015, until its expiry on March 31, 2018.

Ontario’s former financial regulator, the Financial Services Commission of Ontario (FSCO), identified conduct contrary to the MBLAA between 2013 and 2015.

A 2018 settlement with FSCO produced the AMPs, neither of which was paid even after the Minister of Finance issued invoices in September 2019.

The case grew more complex when it emerged that across three successive renewal applications – filed in 2018, 2021, and 2023 – both Ferreira and FIIC answered “No” to questions about past regulatory discipline.

FSRA issued a Notice of Proposal in May 2024 to refuse both applications on grounds of unsuitability, citing the unpaid penalties and those misstatements.

False statements on licence applications have become a recurring element in recent FSRA enforcement files.

A settlement reached December 20, 2024 resolved the matter without a Financial Services Tribunal hearing.

Ferreira agreed to pay the $30,000 AMP, and FIIC withdrew its renewal application.

His insurance agent licence was renewed under two-year conditions: mandatory supervision by a licenced insurance agent with at least two years of experience, a bar on supervising other agents, a prohibition on holding significant control over any licenced insurance corporation, and quarterly written reports to FSRA’s senior manager.

The order was issued January 10, 2025.

A Laval man has been convicted on eight fraud counts after secretly registering high-interest mortgages on properties he had agreed to purchase, leaving homeowners unable to recover what they were owed. https://t.co/B1yeEAer5s — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 5, 2026

Part of a broader enforcement wave

The case arrives as FSRA’s enforcement actions surged across all regulated sectors in 2024–25, with the regulator initiating 100 actions, up from 65 the year prior, and imposing approximately $1.2 million in AMPs – the majority in mortgage brokering.

Elissa Sinha, director of litigation and enforcement at FSRA, wrote in the regulator’s first annual enforcement report that “enforcement is critical to FSRA’s mandate to protect consumers, promote high business standards, and deter fraud and misconduct in regulated sectors.”

Established brokers have welcomed the shift. “I’ve seen more cases against bad actors in the last 12 to 18 months than in previous years,” Joe Sammut, broker of record at Mortgage Architects – A Better Way in Ontario, told Canadian Mortgage Professional in a March interview on FSRA’s tougher enforcement stance.

“They seem to be clamping down and cleaning up, and they’re making sure the fines they’re enacting on people are publicized. They’re finally taking seriously the role we play as mortgage professionals in the transaction. It’s frustrating to see the lack of professionalism [from some mortgage agents]. But I think what the latest regulation is doing is making the good ones even better and the bad ones are that much more obvious.”

Carmen Costa, principal broker at TCG Lending Centres in Ontario, shared a similar view, saying Ontario’s framework is “appropriate, and in many ways necessary” because “strong oversight is important” when dealing with complex financial products that can reshape clients’ finances.

items._ogDesc: The developer’s second receivership in months raises hard questions about Vancouver’s condo future
items.body:
A BC Supreme Court judge has placed a stalled West End condo development under receivership – the second Westbank Holdings Ltd. project to face such action in 2026.

Justice Kevin D. Loo appointed MNP Ltd. as receiver on November 4, after a credit agreement dating to 2016 collapsed under the weight of mounting unpaid debt owed to Bank of Montreal (BMO).

The proceeding, docketed as Bank of Montreal v 700 Bidwell Holdings Inc. (2026 BCSC 2149), names 700 Bidwell Holdings Inc., 700 Bidwell Limited Partnership, 700 Bidwell Property Inc., and Westbank Holdings Ltd.

It follows the April 2026 receivership of Joyce 2, a separate Westbank project.

A decade in the making

The site at 1668 and 1684 Alberni Street in Vancouver’s West End has been in development since August 2017, when a rezoning application was filed for a proposed 40-storey tower containing 128 strata units.

Vancouver City Council approved the rezoning in May 2022, but a development permit application was cancelled in September 2025, the same period in which interest payments under the BMO credit agreement ceased.

Justice Loo set out the financial damage in blunt terms in his written reasons.

“The respondents owe the bank more than $36 million. The respondents have failed to make interest payments when due since at least September 2025, and they have failed to repay the outstanding debt following a demand on January 26, 2026. Since issuance of that demand, the bank debt has increased by over $914,850 in accrued interest, plus costs.”

“At the end of the day, it is clear in this case that the debt is not being paid,” Loo concluded.

The respondents conceded they had made no proposals to repay what was owed, despite earlier promises to do so, and acknowledged the bank had extended repeated opportunities to resolve the defaults, none of which were acted upon.

Interest was accruing at approximately $5,150 per day, with more than $300,000 accumulating since the petition was filed on August 12, 2026. Rental income collected from tenants in the existing buildings had also not been remitted to BMO as required under the agreement.

Loo also flagged the complexity of any potential sale.

“I can infer, despite the paltry evidence in this regard, that any transaction with respect to the lands will not be simple.”

Receiverships rising as Vancouver’s condo market stalls

The ruling arrives as real estate receiverships surge nationally. Lauren White, executive vice-president of CBRE’s land services group in Toronto, identified the structural cause: “These projects that are under construction, they’ve seen such a rise in prices that they just, they run out of money.”

Investor activity in Metro Vancouver’s pre-construction market collapsed from roughly 50% of buyers between 2020 and 2023 to just 7% by 2025, according to Rennie Intelligence data.

“Right now, the market is out of gas,” Ryan Berlin, head economist and vice-president at Rennie Intelligence in Vancouver, previously said.

“Nothing is working for developers. It’s not really working for buyers. So, we’re just kind of stagnating right now.”

Justice Loo gave the respondents until February 13, 2027, to refinance before MNP Ltd. can proceed with any sale.

Westbank says it will appeal. “There is no basis for this filing and we will be submitting an appeal,” the company told CTV News.

“We have no further comment.”

items.title: Insider: Budget 2026 Opens Up Financing For Small Rental Builders
items.description:
A developer who shelved a small rental project over financing has a reason to price it again.

Budget 2026 gives newly built triplexes and fourplexes access to insured loans of up to 90% of completed value. It also lets private insurers cover buildings with five to 50 units.

Budget 2026, tabled November 5, pairs those changes with more money for Build Canada Homes. For a smaller builder, the mortgage rules are the part to take to a lender first: how much cash would the project need up front, and could the finished building support the loan?

Keep the rent assumptions where they were for that comparison. Otherwise, it becomes hard to tell whether the financing has improved the project or the spreadsheet has simply become more optimistic.

Different rules on either side of five units

The Department of Finance's technical rules take effect for insurance applications lenders submit on or after February 1, 2027. The unit count determines which rules apply.

For buildings with five to 50 units, term financing requires a minimum debt coverage ratio of 1.15 for a five-year term or 1.10 for a ten-year term. Borrowers need net worth equal to at least 25% of the requested loan, with a $100,000 minimum, based on Canadian assets. Separately titled properties cannot be bundled to meet the unit requirement.

Construction loans are assessed separately. Insurers set their own debt-servicing criteria during construction; the prescribed amortization and debt coverage requirements apply to term financing. Borrowers using the new three- and four-unit option also have to pass personal qualification tests for the long-term mortgage.

A fourplex and a six-unit building can face quite different borrowing limits on the same site. The six-unit design may qualify for a longer amortization, but it may also cost more to build. Compare the extra debt with the extra cost and rent before choosing the larger project.

Compare the new loans with CMHC

CMHC Standard Rental Housing already covers eligible properties with at least five units. It allows borrowing of up to 85% of value, with amortizations of up to 50 years for new construction and 40 years for existing properties.

MLI Select offers different terms in exchange for commitments to affordability, energy efficiency or accessibility. Eligible new construction can qualify for up to 95% loan-to-cost, depending on the points earned and the program's other requirements.

The new private-insurer rules add another option to that comparison. Be careful with the percentages: 90% of appraised value and 95% of project cost can produce quite different loan amounts.

Ask for offers that cover the same project and construction schedule. Compare the interest rate and insurance premium, then work through guarantees, reserve requirements and conditions on each draw. A larger approved loan can be less useful if its costs are higher or the money arrives too late to pay the contractor.

The rent limits the loan

Take a hypothetical new rental building worth $5 million, with annual net operating income of $225,000. At a 5% mortgage rate, a 50-year amortization and 1.15 debt coverage, the income supports about $3.62 million of debt. A loan at 90% of the building's value would be $4.5 million.

That leaves a gap of roughly $881,000 between the advertised maximum and what the income can support.

Illustrative calculation: a $4.5-million value ceiling versus income-based capacity of about $4.25 million at 4%, $3.62 million at 5% and $3.13 million at 6%. Assumes 50-year amortization and 1.15 debt coverage.

These calculations apply to the mortgage after construction. They use monthly payments and Canadian nominal rates compounded semi-annually, and exclude insurance premiums, fees and reserves. The rates are examples rather than lender quotes. An insurer may also use different income and expense assumptions when it assesses the property.

A builder can tie up less equity and still be taking on more risk. The loan has to be serviced through vacancies, repairs and a slower-than-expected lease-up. Those expenses belong in the operating budget before anyone calculates how much debt the building can carry.

Get the construction loan and the permanent mortgage assessed together. If the finished property cannot support enough mortgage debt to repay the construction lender, the builder has to find the difference.

Build Canada Homes funding starts later

The budget proposes another $13 billion in cash capital for Build Canada Homes over ten years, beginning in 2028–29. That would bring its capitalization to $45 billion. Ottawa's target is 200,000 homes over the next decade; delivery will depend on projects moving through approvals and construction.

It also proposes $1.5 billion over four years from 2027–28 for infrastructure on federal land, plus $387.4 million in later years. A builder considering a partnership needs to know when a particular site will be serviced and when the money will be available. Procurement terms will determine who can take part.

Source: Department of Finance missing-middle backgrounder and Budget 2026 Chapter 3, November 5, 2026. Fiscal-year funding starts are not home-completion dates.

Public land and long-term capital can help build housing for people whose rents cannot cover the cost of new construction. The operating budget needs funding, too. Taxes, maintenance and repairs continue long after the building opens.

For market rental projects, the effect will depend partly on the supply of buildable sites. Easier financing can help developers start viable projects. Where land and approvals are scarce, buyers may instead use the extra borrowing room to bid more for the same sites.

Reprice the project before bidding more for land

Run the available financing options against the same operating budget. Then confirm which lenders and insurers will offer them, what they need to approve an application and how the construction loan converts to a term mortgage. February 1 is the start date for lender submissions, so allow time for approval and funding.

For a small developer, the useful result is a loan commitment that makes a viable project possible.

If the numbers work only after raising the projected rents or cutting the repair allowance, the financing problem is still there.

items.body:
Time for your cheat sheet on this week’s top stories.

Canadian Real Estate

Canada To Lift Ban On Foreign Buyers of New Homes For “Affordability”

Canada’s Budget 2026 will extend the foreign buyer home ban but exempt new homes. Billions in taxpayer back incentives were used to create supply with the narrative of bringing prices lower. Now that developers are sitting on near record inventory that’s still out of reach for local incomes, the plan has changed. Policymakers argue demand from non-residents will boost affordability by helping to create new supply. The problem? The ban was extended because non-resident speculators were flooding into new homes in the first place.

Canadian Unemployment Climbs, Nearly 1 in 3 Struggle To Buy Necessities

Headline employment data looked largely unchanged but the devil was in the details. Statistics Canada (StatCan) reported jobs were relatively unchanged in October. Unemployment still climbed 0.2 points to 6.7% though, as more people sought work. The worst news was in a special supplement that revealed almost 1 in 3 struggle to pay for necessities, rolling back improvements made since 2022. The headline may show little change in jobs, but the details show more unemployment for longer terms, and less financial security.

The Data Center Boom: Internet Landlords & A $3 Trillion Real Estate Bubble

Investors in both Canada and the US are planning a lot of data centers. The rising and revolutionary use of AI means more will be needed, but just how many? Crunching the numbers reveals that just 1 in 5 data centers announced have actual progress. Investors and the politicians they’ve elected are blaming an energy shortage, but we found most haven’t applied for a utilities hookup. We take a deep dive into the multi-trillion speculative data center real estate bubble and the tax changes that have them vying to become landlords of the internet.

Canadian Banks Brace For Mortgage Losses, 3x Pre-Pandemic Share

Banks are bracing themselves for the fallout from Canada’s real estate bubble popping. The bank’s median allowance for mortgage losses has climbed 138.1% over the past 4 years, tripling since Q2 2019. The top 25% of banks preparing for losses has set aside nearly double the median, and the most since 2015. While economists at many banks are saying the bottom is near, their risk departments are preparing for it to worsen in the near-term.

Toronto Real Estate

Toronto Real Estate Prices Have Dropped Over $360k Since Peak

The price of a typical home in Greater Toronto slipped 0.1% to $915,400 in October. Losses extended further as weak sales and lofty inventory combined to create further downward pressure. This likely surprises many, as prices have already trimmed 28.4% (-$363k) from the 2022 peak. However, the supply balance suggests things may get worse before they improve.

Vancouver Real Estate

Vancouver Real Estate Prices Slip, Just 3% Higher Than 2017 Peak

The price of a home across Greater Vancouver fell 0.7% to $1.07 million in October, 5.2% lower than last year. Weak sales and lofty inventory has pushed the region out of stagnation and into a second-leg of a correction. How low can prices go? It’s not clear, but it’s worth noting that at this level, the price of a typical home is only 3% higher than it was at the 2017 peak. Nearly a decade of stagnation and the market’s indicators are slanted towards further declines.

items.body:
Canada has one weird trick to help with housing affordability—sell the new homes you can’t afford to foreign buyers. That’s not a mistake; it’s the pitch in Canada’s Budget 2026, which will extend the foreign buyer ban until 2029. However, this time they plan to exempt foreign buyers to clear the stagnating inventory. Ottawa frames this as a win for affordability despite all evidence suggesting otherwise.

Canada To Allow Foreign Buying of New Homes For “Affordability”

Canada’s existing ban on foreign ownership is set to expire in just under two months. Despite quietly inserting exemptions in the ban just 86 days after the law took effect, policymakers say they’ll renew the policy. Sort of.

“[Canada will] extend the ban on foreign purchases of existing residential properties for two years, to January 1, 2029, while exempting new residential properties,” reads Budget 2026.

That’s right. Policymakers plan to reopen foreign buying of new homes, the segment that sparked the ban in the first place. The doublespeak doesn’t end there.

“This would help protect housing affordability by keeping the vast majority of the market available for Canadians, while unlocking additional investment in new housing supply,” explains Budget 2026.

Ottawa Wants Foreign Investment To Help Build More Housing

More supply was supposed to bring down prices, but that didn’t happen. Billions in tax incentives stimulated building new supply, but prices remain out of reach. New home sales in cities like Toronto are near record lows, while developers sit on record inventory. Weak demand hasn’t brought prices down much—in fact, home prices are near highs in most provinces. With home prices requiring nearly double the median household income to buy at these levels, Canadians can’t afford to buy a home.

Despite years of warnings that weak sales will slow construction, new building remains elevated. In fact, elsewhere in Budget 2026, policymakers boasted about their contribution to roughly 250,000 annualized new home starts in the first half of 2026, 20% above the 2015-2019 average. However, the narrative of slow sales threatening new home construction has seen taxpayers back billions in developer bailouts. Now Ottawa is hoping foreign buyers will be a further bailout for developers.

Foreign Buyers Were Concentrated In New Homes Before The Ban

Policymakers may be claiming that ignorance is strength, and the foreign buyer ban was always to target existing stock. But a quick trip down the data memory lane makes it clear pretty fast that new homes were the primary issue.

The 2020 property records that led Ottawa to create the ban show a concentration in new condos (post-2016 builds). Almost 1 in 7 (13.4%) of BC’s new condos were owned by non-residents that year, the highest among the four provinces studied. Non-residents also piled into Nova Scotia (11.1%), New Brunswick (10%), and Ontario (9.2%). Most of these new condos were in major cities.

Toronto may sound light with non-residents owning 7.7% of new condos, according to 2019 property records. However, keep in mind the region represented 1 in 6 home sales across Canada then. Even so, it looks tiny in contrast to the 13.6% in Vancouver. Of course, Canada’s current housing minister MP Gregor Robertson doesn’t need a refresher—the Vancouver-based minister was the Mayor of Vancouver at the peak of its foreign buying boom.

Despite arguing in favour of foreign capital in housing recently, he sang a different tune back then. Back in 2016, he blasted the Province for not imposing taxes to slow buying. “Middle-class Canadians being able to buy a house in Vancouver and Toronto, those days have probably passed because the [foreign buyer] interventions didn’t come,” said then-Mayor Robertson.

Well, if middle-class families can’t afford housing in the rest of Canada now, why not go all in?

Canada Wants Its Foreign Buyers Back, But Will They Return?

First off, when Canada says “non-resident investment,” it almost entirely means Chinese investors, representing roughly 70% of that demand. These buyers were driven by a reputation of a financial system free from political persecution, wealthy students looking for prestigious education, and a scramble of capital looking to be laundered in Canadian housing—much of it fleeing China’s anti-corruption crackdown.

Vancouver’s foreign home buyer boom began when wealthy Hong Kongers sought investment safety. Canada’s financial system is no longer viewed as a system free from political persecution. The shift extends beyond Canada, with Beijing advising China’s elites to pull their investments out of Western countries. The country recently tightened outbound investment even further.

China used to be Canada’s number one source of international students. Canada has since traded in its prestigious reputation for one better known as a back door to immigration. China has since gone from being the number one source of foreign students to falling behind Guinea. Maybe Guinean students will fuel the new housing demand.

The opaque system that made Canadian real estate the perfect asset for money laundering has also since come under scrutiny. The use of Canada’s banks to launder money through real estate was well known, facilitating billions in transfers. Canadian banks have since received a few slaps on the wrist, paid billions in fines, and come under much tighter oversight. Darn it. Why are regulators so anti-supply, preventing affordability!

None of this is to say that Canada won’t see a rise in the number of foreign buyers. However, it’s unlikely to be from the source that drove investor demand before. A new market may be developing, especially since it’s common to sell new homes cheaper overseas to prevent local prices from falling. That might even be more enticing if Vancouver’s Condo King negotiated the foreign buyer tax incentives he was working on with the PM.

items._ogDesc: Canada's employment stalled in October as the unemployment rate climbed to 6.7%. StatCan warns nearly 1 in 3 adults now struggle to afford basic necessities.
items.body:
Canadian employment was little changed last month, but the details were more concerning. Statistics Canada (StatCan) data show employment stalled in October, but unemployment climbed. It’s not just harder to find a job, but those unemployed are struggling to find work. The agency warns that nearly 1 in 3 adults now face financial hardship, rolling back gains made since 2022.

Canadian Employment Stalls As Unemployment Climbs

Canadian seasonally adjusted unemployment rate.

Employment was virtually flat (0%; -4.7k) in October, following losses in September (-68k) and August (-42k). Despite the stall, more people searching for work pushed the unemployment rate to 6.7%, up 0.2 points. Most of the pain is concentrated in Alberta and Ontario, where the rate is now 7.3% in both provinces.

October’s flat move somewhat downplays the emerging weakness in the labour force. A sharp drop in private sector employment (-53k) was only offset by a jump in the public sector (+50k). The public sector’s increase comes after four months of losses.

Employment has only grown 0.1% (+17k) over the past year. That’s a little light considering population revisions show 189.4k more people y/y in Q3. StatCan has previously stated that the revisions will be gradually introduced into employment data. Dismissing slow growth due to the population no longer makes sense, and unemployment is understated.

Retail Leads Job Losses, While Construction Adds Workers

The areas most impacted were wholesale and retail (-1.0%; -29k jobs) in October, contracting 3.7% (-113k) in the past year. Those losses were partially offset by construction growing 0.9% (+16k) in October, rising 2.9% (+47k) in the past year.

One surprise in the data is education, which grew 1.0% (+15k) in October. This partially reverses the 35k jobs lost in the sector in September, but it remains 3.0% (-48k) lower than last year.

Nearly 30% Of Canadians Struggle to Cover Necessities

The share of Canadians who struggled to pay for necessities, including transportation, housing, food, and clothing.

A lot more Canadians are struggling, according to StatCan’s special supplement. The agency’s labour report also had numbers on the share of those aged 15+ struggling to pay for necessities. They found 29.7% of people had difficulty paying for necessities in the past four weeks, up 2 points from last year. This recent bump partially rolls back improvements made from 2022 through 2025.

Among Canada’s 15 CMAs, the worst hit is Oshawa, where 38.4% of people struggled to buy necessities. It was followed by Windsor (36.9%) and Hamilton (35.9%). The trio makes it easy to conclude this is trade war-related, but it may be an Ontario thing. Even more diversified regions like Toronto (32%) were much higher than Vancouver (26.1%). Though, to be fair, 1 in 4 adults struggling to pay for necessities is still a systemic failure.

Struggling to find a job after a loss is definitely a contributor. Only 18.9% of those unemployed in September found work in October, well below the 24.6% in the same period from 2017 to 2019. Long-term unemployment (27+ weeks) also hit 23.7%, up from 21.5% last year and an average of just 17.2% between 2017 and 2019, warns StatCan.

Headline employment shows a stall, but clearly that’s an overly optimistic view. The population continues to grow faster than the handful of jobs being created. Replacing a lost job is harder, and long-term unemployment is spreading to more people. Add to that the reversal in financial security improvements, and this is one of the worst reports in a while.

items.title: Fraser Academy Buys Old LaSalle College Campus In Vancouver For $35M
items.description:
The low-rise office building that was formerly home to private post-secondary arts and design school LaSalle College was sold over the summer, according to transaction data seen by STOREYS.

The property is located at 2665 Renfrew Street in Vancouver, at the northwest corner of the intersection with Bradfield Court, and one block north from E 12th Avenue and the Millennium Line SkyTrain’s Renfrew Station.

Originally constructed in 1990, the two-storey building was home to The Art Institute of Vancouver, which was acquired in January 2017 by Montreal-based LCI Education, the parent company of LaSalle College. The Art Institute of Vancouver was subsequently rebranded as LaSalle College Vancouver.

In 2018, LaSalle College Vancouver retained commercial real estate services company Colliers to find them a new home.

Local developer Molnar Group subsequently acquired 2665 Renfrew Street, and the parking lot at 2710 Renfrew Street, for $73,500,000 from Aikang Capital Inc. LaSalle, Colliers, and Molnar then negotiated a pre-lease and build-to-suit agreement to move LaSalle College out of 2665 Renfrew Street and into the new office complex — named The Kaslo — Molnar Group was developing at 2710 Kaslo Street.

The Kaslo consists of two seven-storey office buildings with around 218,000 sq. ft of office space. LaSalle College Vancouver occupies the East Tower — about 108,000 sq. ft — and moved into the new building in 2025.

This summer, Molnar Group then sold the old campus at 2665 Renfrew Street for $35,000,000. BC Assessment values 2665 Renfrew Street at $36,678,000 in its latest assessment, which is dated to July 1, 2025. According to BC Assessment, the building is home to 68,781 sq. ft of space, thus the sale price translates to $509 per sq. ft.

The Fraser Academy

The purchaser was the Fraser Academy, a private, non-profit special needs school. The Fraser Academy previously communicated in February that it was looking for a new home, whether that be redeveloping their existing home at 2294 W 10th Ave in Vancouver, near Kitsilano Secondary School, or finding a new building to move to.

On September 3, Fraser Academy announced that they are relocating to 2665 Renfrew Street, noting that no tuition funds were used to fund the purchase. The new building will also be home to The Centre for Dyslexia, which will provide access to specialized learning support for children, youth, and adults with dyslexia, families, and training for educators across Canada.

A rendering of Fraser Academy’s new campus. (Fraser Academy)

“By purchasing the Renfrew property, we are investing in a permanent home that builds long-term value for our community, something we could not achieve on leased land at West 10th Avenue,” they said. “Rather than embarking on a costly and complex new build, we are able to renovate an existing, spacious two-storey facility, making the most of our resources and reducing both costs and risks along the way.”

“This approach gives us the flexibility to design spaces that truly support our dyslexic learners — think spacious classrooms, enhanced learning areas, and a future gym — all while sparing our students and families from years of construction delays or temporary moves,” the Fraser Academy added.

The renovation process is expected to commence in January 2027 and the new campus is expected to be ready by September 2027. The Fraser Academy has retained SSDG Interiors and VPAC Construction Group for the renovations.

LaSalle College

In February, a syndicate of banks including RBC, BMO, and CIBC retained Deloitte to review the financial operations of LCI Group, the parent company of LaSalle College.

LCI Group operates a network of 11 private higher education institutions in Canada, as well as in Spain, Australia, Morocco, Colombia, and Costa Rica. Altogether it operates 14 campuses across five continents, offers 55 programs across seven fields of study, and has approximately 3,000 students enrolled in its programs.

On August 24, LaSalle College sought and obtained creditor protection under the federal Companies’ Creditors Arrangement Act (CCAA), but the proceedings are only pertaining to the corporate entities that own LaSalle College Montreal, according to court documents. LaSalle College Vancouver is held under a different corporate entity and is not subject to the proceedings.

“Over the past several years, LaSalle College has faced significant and recurring liquidity constraints resulting from, among other things, declining [enrolment], regulatory pressures and financial penalties and operating losses,” said the court-appointed Monitor. “These pressures have materially impaired LaSalle College’s ability to meet its obligations as they become due and to fund its operations without further financial support.”

The creditor protection proceeding remains ongoing, but the school remains operational and students returned to class in September after a brief delay.

The price of a typical home across Greater Vancouver.

Source: GVREB; CREA; Better Dwelling.

The price of a typical home fell 0.7% (-$7.3k) to $1.07 million in October, 5.2% (-$58.5k) lower than last year. Since the 2022 peak, they’ve plunged 14.7% (-$184.2k) to the weakest level since March 2021. While prices initially resisted a Toronto-sized correction, they’ve consistently been grinding lower. As of last month, prices were just 3.1% (+$32.5k) higher than the 2017 cycle peak. That’s pretty much 9 years of stagnation.

Vancouver Home Sales Fall To Correction Levels

Greater Vancouver existing home sales.

Source: GVREB; CREA; Better Dwelling.

The demand slump continued, with the board reporting just 2,024 sales in October, 10.2% lower than last year. October sales are never high, but this scale of weakness is rare outside of market slumps. It’s a level consistent with those in 2022, 2018, and 2012—not exactly years the industry is longing to relive.

Vancouver New Listings Slip, But Overall Inventory Remains Strong

Fewer sellers hit the market last month. There were 4,805 new listings in October, down 11.6% from last year and a 3-year low for the month. However, lower doesn’t mean low—this is a surprisingly healthy volume for the region. It’s an elevated level that’s rarely seen outside of slumps.

Vancouver Real Estate Inventory Remains Unusually Strong

Active listings of homes for sale across Greater Vancouver.

Source: GVREB; CREA; Better Dwelling.

Stagnating inventory may be part of the reason no one’s in a rush to list their home for sale. There were 15,688 active listings in October, down 4.3% from last year, when the market set a 13-year high for the month. To be blunt, the drop was from a very high place, and still marked one of the highest volumes on record. The downward pressure on prices was further amplified by the fact that sales dropped at a faster rate.

Home prices in Greater Vancouver are having a crisis of value. While the market didn’t drop to the same extent as Toronto, it also failed three attempts to move higher. Buyers in the region are resistant to higher prices, and it’s unclear how much prices need to fall to get them to jump in. Meanwhile, the market is approaching nearly 10 years of stagnation.

 A monthly report from Rentals.

items.body:
TORONTO — The average asking price for a rental unit across Canada in October was $2,036, down 3.2 per cent compared with a year ago.

A monthly report from Rentals.ca and Urbanation says October's decrease marks the smallest year-over-year decline since February, when rents were down 2.8 per cent from the same month a year earlier.

Average asking rents have now fallen year-over-year for 25 consecutive months, with prices down 5.4 per cent compared with two years ago and reaching their lowest October level since 2022.

Rents were essentially flat on a monthly basis, edging 0.1 per cent higher from September.

Urbanation president Shaun Hildebrand says the window for cheaper rents is closing in Toronto and Vancouver as prices are starting to rise for the first time in nearly three years amid declining supply, while renters still hold the advantage in Calgary, Edmonton and much of Ontario, where prices continue to fall.

Asking rents for purpose-built apartments fell 2.1 per cent year-over-year to an average of $2,040 last month, while asking rents for condominium apartments decreased 5.5 per cent to $2,048.

items.title: Lower Prices Softening The Hit Of Higher Borrowing Costs For GTA Buyers
items.description:
Borrowing costs in the Greater Toronto Area are higher than they were a year ago.

Even so, the monthly mortgage payment on an average-priced home has only edged up, and it’s still well below what buyers were paying in 2023 and 2024, according to the latest from the Toronto Regional Real Estate Board (TRREB).

“GTA homebuyers continued to benefit from substantial negotiating power on price over the past year. While borrowing costs have increased on the back of higher inflation, the impact on monthly mortgage payments has been mitigated by lower selling prices, helping keep affordability in check,” said TRREB Chief Information Officer Jason Mercer.

Prices have continued to fall from last year’s levels. In October, the MLS® Home Price Index (MLS® HPI) Composite benchmark was 4.3% lower than a year earlier. The average selling price came in at $1,024,108, down 2.7%.

Even with lower prices, many buyers are still holding back. TRREB says they’re uncertain about where inflation, borrowing costs and the economy are headed.

There were 5,603 home sales through TRREB’s MLS® System in October, 7.9% fewer than in October 2025. New listings dropped to 14,173, down 11.9% year-over-year.

The month-to-month picture looks different. With seasonal adjustment, sales, new listings, the HPI Composite and the average selling price all moved up from September.

TRREB President Daniel Steinfeld said a clearer economic picture could bring buyers back in the new year.

“If a Canada-U.S. trade deal is reached, GTA residents could gain a clearer picture of the economic outlook. Combined with a resolution to the conflict in the Middle East, this could help ease concerns about inflation and economic uncertainty, strengthen consumer confidence and renew interest in homeownership as we move into 2027,” said Steinfeld.

TRREB CEO John DiMichele took a longer view.

“While we continue to experience shorter-term volatility in the ownership housing market, we can’t lose track of the fact that the permanent population will continue to grow in our region. Policy announcements, including HST rebates and development charge reductions should help bring a greater diversity of ownership and rental supply online in the medium-term to ensure new families are properly and affordably housed,” said DiMichele.

items.title: Housing experts urge B.C. to rethink development charges
items.description: U.S., U.K., Australia offer different approaches to paying for infrastructure
items._ogDesc: U.S., U.K., Australia offer different approaches to paying for infrastructure
items.body:
With Metro Vancouver condo construction hitting a 15-year low amid rising costs and slower demand, some housing experts and developers say it may be time to revisit development charges and consider alternative ways to fund municipal infrastructure.

Development charges are fees municipalities levy on developers when they build new homes or other projects. The money helps pay for infrastructure needed to support new development, such as roads, water and sewer pipes, drainage, parks and community facilities.

However, what were originally modest charges have increased “at an alarming rate” in many Canadian municipalities, including in B.C., according to the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC).

“It started as an earmarked tax that is very focused and determined on a specific purpose. But over time what happened is they started to fund more and more different purposes,” said Mathieu Laberge, chief economist at CMHC.

“[Development charges] now in some centres are used to fund public libraries, firefighting services or police services, daycare.”

A 2023 report by the Urban Development Institute found that government taxes and fees, including development charges, can account for about 29 per cent of the purchase price of a new condo unit in Vancouver.

“Ultimately it's embedded in the price of new homes and it's passed on to buyers,” said Laberge.

In June, Ontario and the federal government launched an $8.8-billion development charge reduction program. Participating municipalities must commit to reducing development charges by at least 30-50 per cent for three years, and federal and provincial funding helps replace some lost municipal revenue.

Michael Waters, CEO of Ottawa-based Minto Group, which has multiple projects under construction in B.C., said he believes similar initiatives are needed in B.C. to help lower building costs and encourage more development.

“Voters get a property tax bill every year. They can see the rate at which their property taxes have gone up,” said Waters.

“It's not as apparent what development charges are or how the rate at which they climbed from year to year. And so they don't typically attract the same level of scrutiny in municipal politics.”

Alternative funding models

Revisiting development charges raises questions about their role in funding municipal infrastructure and how municipalities would make up any shortfall if the fees were reduced.

Andrew Sancton, professor emeritus of political science at Western University, said the “old-fashioned way” is for municipalities to borrow money to build new infrastructure projects, then pay those loans back through property taxes collected or utility charges.

“In most places, the cost of new infrastructure is paid for by everybody, not by just the people who are purchasing new buildings,” he said. “And development charges have replaced that method in many ways.”

For example, if a new wastewater plant is needed in a developing area, a municipality could borrow the money to build it and it will be paid back over time through revenue from users of the system, Sancton said.

He pointed to tax increment financing. Under this model, a municipality can finance an infrastructure project upfront and repay the debt using increases in property-tax revenue generated within a designated area as it develops.

Waters said other countries have adopted different mechanisms to funding growth-related infrastructure that could inspire some ideas for B.C.

In England, some local authorities use the Community Infrastructure Levy, a charge on eligible new development that helps fund infrastructure needed to support growth. Some U.S. municipalities use special district financing, issuing bonds to cover upfront infrastructure costs and repaying them through taxes or assessments on properties within designated areas.

In New South Wales, Australia, a standardized Housing and Productivity Contribution helps fund state and regional infrastructure, including major roads, public transit, schools and hospitals, while municipalities continue to collect separate contributions for local infrastructure.

“I'm not saying any of these are a silver bullet or a way that you can replace [development charges] entirely, but could they be used to complement or, in concert with development charges, to make the sharing of infrastructure costs more equitable?” said Waters.

Quebec and Alberta are using a different tax mix instead of development charges, according to Laberge. For example, Quebec municipalities can borrow money and issue municipal bonds to finance capital projects, including infrastructure.

But Laberge noted that even if development charges are reduced significantly or even eliminated, it wouldn't be sufficient to resolve the supply gap observed across the province.

“Other things need to be done as well, and other factors involved. We need to look at development charges, but also more broadly, red tape and how we build.”

items.title: Victoria's Market Square is on the market for $25M
items.description: The collection of heritage buildings around an open-air courtyard is on half a city block bordered by Pandora Avenue, Store Street and Johnson Street.
items._ogDesc: The collection of heritage buildings around an open-air courtyard is on half a city block bordered by Pandora Avenue, Store Street and Johnson Street.
items.body:
A prime 1.5-acre swath of downtown Victoria is on the market for $25 million.

Market Square, a collection of heritage buildings around an open-air courtyard on half a city block bordered by Pandora Avenue, Store Street and Johnson Street, was listed for sale this week.

The owners, Vancouver-based Anthem Properties, acquired the property more than 20 years ago.

Commercial real estate agent Matt Pettinger said a number of groups have expressed interest in acquiring Market Square.

“Market Square is one of those properties that almost everyone in the Victoria area is familiar with,” said Pettinger, a senior vice-president with Avison Young. “Opportunities to acquire an asset of this profile in the downtown core don’t come along very often.”

Market Square was established in the 1970s by brothers Sam and Nick Bawlf.

The project, according to Canada’s Historic Places, was an attempt to reactivate a depressed downtown core and breathe new life into historic buildings, including the Milne Block in the 500-block of Johnson Street that was built in 1891.

All of the buildings were built between 1890 and 1912 and the property covers just under 1.5 acres.

There is a total leasable space of more than 95,000 square feet, including 56,775 square feet of retail space and 38,658 square feet of office space.

Less than 10 per cent of the total leasable space is currently vacant, Pettinger said, adding most of that is office space.

The square provides a net operating income of $1.94 million annually, and includes Famoso Italian Pizzeria, Café Mexico, The Drake Eatery, Whistle Buoy Brewing and Pacific Rim College as its major tenants.

Pettinger said any potential buyers will have to sign a non-disclosure agreement to get access to information on leases and other details.

Market Square is the second high-profile stretch of the downtown to hit the market this fall.

In September, the two-storey Broad Street Square at 1290 Broad St. was listed for sale, with an asking price of $10.95 million.

The 25,000-square-foot building occupies half of the 1200-block on the west side of Broad Street and a long stretch of the 600-block of Yates Street.

items.title: New hotel design pitched for burned Plaza site in downtown Victoria
items.description: Tech company Redbrick has unveiled its plan for a 198-room, 17-storey hotel at the corner of Government Street and Pandora Avenue.
items._ogDesc: Tech company Redbrick has unveiled its plan for a 198-room, 17-storey hotel at the corner of Government Street and Pandora Avenue.
items.body:
The new owner of the downtown Victoria property where a massive fire destroyed the Plaza Hotel seven years ago is taking another run at building a new hotel on the site.

Victoria tech company Redbrick unveiled its designs this week for a 198-room, 17-storey hotel at the corner of Government Street and Pandora Avenue.

The Plaza burned to the ground on May 6, 2019, in a blaze determined to have been sparked by arson.

The high-profile site across from the McPherson Playhouse, Centennial Square and city hall has remained vacant behind a high plywood wall ever since, despite an effort by another developer to build a hotel on the property.

A proposal for a 12-storey, 200-room hotel was declined by Victoria city council last year, on the grounds that the proposed height and density didn’t fit in with the neighbourhood.

Oceangate Developments and Mairet Hotels said in January that it had lost confidence that the project could proceed, and sold the property to Redbrick for an undisclosed amount.

Redbrick chief executive Tobyn Sowden said the new plan is for a heritage-style four-storey podium structure that would fit in with neighbouring Old Town buildings, topped by a floor for an indoor and outdoor spa, then a 12-storey tower.

The total height of the proposed building is 64.5 metres, including a rooftop restaurant and bar with a view of the harbour.

Sowden said the hotel still needs about 200 rooms to be viable, but the podium design would make it a better fit within the neighbourhood, which is largely made up of two- and three-storey buildings.

The glass tower, meanwhile, would be set back off Government Street, “so you don’t feel that sheer height as you’re walking as a pedestrian alongside a historic-style podium.”

An open house at Redbrick’s Douglas Street headquarters on Tuesday and a new website are the first steps in gathering public feedback before the company takes its proposal to city council, likely by the end of the year.

Redbrick is partnering with Victoria builder Aryze and Seattle-based architect Olson Kundig on the project, which includes a plaza courtyard on city-owned land with widened sidewalks, pedestrian walkways, seating and landscaping. The project also includes a spa with outdoor gardens along the podium’s second floor, and four levels of underground parking.

Sowden is calling it the Westholme after the lumber company that built the original hotel on the site in 1911.

The Westholme Hotel was one of Victoria’s largest hotels at the time, with a 600-seat dining room and a dance floor with room for an orchestra. The building had numerous other names and uses over the years, including as a country and western bar and one of the city’s last strip clubs.

Sowden said Westholme built the hotel to diversify from its lumber business, and Redbrick is essentially doing the same by rebuilding a hotel in the same neighbourhood where he has built his own business over the last 15 years.

Sowden called the proposed hotel a “gateway” to the industry, arts and innovation district the city is developing at the north end of downtown. Residential development is planned around the Capital Iron lands, and the Art Gallery of Greater Victoria could eventually move into the area.

“It’s going to push commerce further down Government Street,” said Sowden. “We want it to be that connection to Chinatown and have tourists go further while at the same time having locals make it their destination, like see a show at the McPherson and having a bite or a drink at the Westholme.”

Sowden said the proposal also responds to a critical need for visitor accommodations, with the region’s hotel supply having dropped nearly 25% since 2016.

The Greater Victoria Hotel Development Working Group estimates that 2,000 net new hotel rooms will be needed over the next decade. The city’s Official Community Plan is targeting 1,500 new hotel rooms by 2035.

items.title: Repealing B.C. housing legislation would be a mistake, says UBC expert
items.description: VICTORIA — A glut of empty condos in British Columbia should not be seen as evidence that the market is working, said a housing expert who warned against winding back policies of the outgoing NDP government designed to tame prices and rent.
items._ogDesc: VICTORIA — A glut of empty condos in British Columbia should not be seen as evidence that the market is working, said a housing expert who warned against winding back policies of the outgoing NDP government designed to tame prices and rent.
items.body:
VICTORIA — A glut of empty condos in British Columbia should not be seen as evidence that the market is working, said a housing expert who warned against winding back policies of the outgoing NDP government designed to tame prices and rent.

Alexandra Flynn, who teaches housing policy at the University of B.C., said the province still needs a lot of homes for low-to very-low-income residents, despite the thousands of empty units.

"We do have a number of empty condos, but market housing for above-average income earners is not the housing we need," she said. Left alone, the market cannot supply affordable and deeply affordable housing, she added.

"If you asked any developer, they would tell you, absent some kind of government intervention and granting and funding, they are not going to be able to do it."

Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson has promised to repeal key aspects of the provincial housing legislation introduced by the outgoing government of Premier David Eby.

"We will return housing decisions to the people and the communities, who know their neighbourhoods so much better than Victoria," Doerkson said during the inaugural meeting of the Conservative caucus.

Doerkson was referring to the proposed repeal of Bill 44, which New Democrats consider their signature piece of housing legislation.

The legislation legalized higher densities on single-lot properties in municipalities with populations above 5,000 people, but also came with housing targets, which have been heavily criticized by local governments.

Sarrah Storey, president of the Union of the British Columbia Municipalities, said Bill 44 was "highly problematic" and municipalities pushed back because the government imposed it as a "one-size-fits-all model" without getting input.

Storey said UBCM agrees with the idea that housing policy for Williams Lake should not be made in Victoria, but if government wants to make changes to Bill 44, it should give municipalities choice.

"There are some local governments that will want to remain with the policies that are in place, allowing multiple homes on single family lots, for example, and they should be able to do so," she said.

Storey, who is the mayor for Fraser Lake, said any housing plan must also consider infrastructure needs.

"I say the best way to support developers is to ensure that the local governments can direct development to areas that are ready to support growth," she said.

Flynn disagrees with the plan to repeal, saying the law can be a "powerful tool," and while some of it needs to be fixed, it would be a mistake to just throw it away.

"If I was the new government, I would not be making any knee-jerk reactions right now," she said.

Flynn said she understands criticism from municipalities, saying there was "no question" that the dialogue between municipalities and Victoria must be improved.

"The province should not be dictating what municipalities do without actually engaging and having the bilateral relationships that are appropriate," Flynn said.

She said housing in British Columbia is in a better place now than it was in 2017 for lots of reasons.

They include the work of the non-profit housing sector, municipalities, the federal government, and the provincial government, she said.

"So, the NDP government introduced some of the most transformative housing reforms in Canada," she said.

Changing circumstances over time do not negate the fact that municipalities need to ensure affordable housing can be built in their communities, she said.

"This is not the time to be thinking about what to repeal," she said. "It's a time to set the course for a new agenda moving forward."

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 4, 2026.

Wolfgang Depner, The Canadian Press

items.title: This $1.7M Vancouver home was auctioned for half the price — but there's a catch
items.description:
VANCOUVER — The home on Windsor Street in East Vancouver has admittedly seen better days. 
 Its yard is overgrown, the weathered shingles are barely hanging on in places, and the back stairs have completely disintegrated.
items._ogDesc: VANCOUVER — The home on Windsor Street in East Vancouver has admittedly seen better days. Its yard is overgrown, the weathered shingles are barely hanging on in places, and the back stairs have completely disintegrated.
items.body:
VANCOUVER — The home on Windsor Street in East Vancouver has admittedly seen better days.

Its yard is overgrown, the weathered shingles are barely hanging on in places, and the back stairs have completely disintegrated.

But with an official BC Assessment valuation of more than $1.7 million, the house appeared to represent a bargain when it sold for $825,000 at Vancouver's annual tax auction at city hall on Wednesday. It had a reserve price of just $72,051.

It was among more than 60 properties auctioned off in this year's City of Vancouver tax sale, set off by owners who have not paid their taxes for three years in a row, with the reserve, or upset prices, set at the amounts owed to the city.

If East Vancouver is not to your taste, then perhaps Point Grey Road? It's one of the most exclusive addresses in Canada, where neighbours include Lululemon billionaire Chip Wilson, whose $73-million home is the most valuable in B.C.

A few blocks down the road from Wilson are two side-by-side houses valued around $5 million and $6 million. They are steps from Jericho Beach and the Royal Vancouver Yacht Club, and sold for less than half their values at $2 million and $2.75 million respectively.

There is, of course, a catch.

After auction day, the current owners have a year to redeem their property by paying their taxes, resulting in a refund to the bidder — plus interest at the rate of six per cent, far in excess of government bond yields or bank interest.

Ron Usher, a retired notary public, said tax auctions are "not for the faint of heart or the inexperienced."

"I suspect some of these tax sales are more whoops than deliberate," Usher said, citing situations such as inheritances.

"You can imagine the law is very much structured to give the maximum possible opportunity for the owner to sort out the problem," Usher said.

Though a posting last week included 116 properties listed for auction, by the time it began at 10 a.m. Wednesday, only 66 remained. Owners of three more properties paid their taxes while the auction was ongoing and the homes were removed from the block.

Vancouverite Darius Wu attended the auction "mostly for fun, hoping I'd get a bargain."

The 30-year-old likened the auction to buying a lottery ticket, but better.

"In a lottery, you lose money no matter what. Here, I would say, the odds are probably one in a hundred. You don't lose any money, and if you win, it's still … pretty good."

It was Wu's first auction in Vancouver, but he ducked out before noon after concluding he wouldn't outbid others in attendance.

"I think there are way more serious people here," he said, noting many of the bids were climbing to around half of the property value listed. "You need a lot of cash to actually participate here."

As the auction dragged on, most of those who earlier jockeyed for a spot inside the chambers trickled out, with the attendees dwindling to about a dozen.

Among them was a man who cast winning bids on dozens of properties, including the home on Windsor Street. Though he declined an interview, he said he didn't expect to be transferred the properties — he would instead collect the interest.

Winning bids are secured by paying the upset price. If the original owner pays their overdue tax within a year, the bidder is refunded the upset price with interest of six per cent. But if it is not redeemed after a year, the bidder takes ownership after paying the balance of their bid within 30 days.

Sean Holden, a longtime Vancouver Realtor, called bidding at the auction "an exercise in futility."

He said he often steers clients away from the auction. When asked if he has ever attended himself, his response is quick.

"I wouldn't waste my time," he said through a chuckle.

Holden points out that tax auction sales that go through to completion are very rare.

But they do happen, both in Vancouver and other B.C. municipalities that conduct their auctions every September on properties with two years of unpaid taxes.

Three properties have changed hands in the last five years in Burnaby, while the City of Vancouver said in a statement that there "were only three instances in the last 10 years where a property changed hands from a tax sale."

"The property taxes on almost all properties have historically been paid within the one-year redemption period," the statement said.

The City of Vancouver tells potential buyers not to trespass, but recommends people do their own research before bidding, noting in a posting last week that it is not responsible for the condition or quality of the homes.

"Prospective purchasers are urged to research the properties and make all necessary inquiries to municipal and other government departments to determine the existence of any bylaws, restriction, charges or other conditions which may affect the value or suitability of the properties," it says.

Holden, who has been a Realtor in the city for about three decades, said that adds risk for the buyer.

"You don't know what condition it will be, and (if) the sellers are forced out by the bank, whether they knock holes in the wall or do other strange things. You're taking a huge risk," he said.

All properties auctioned on Wednesday received bids. Only one property was sold for the upset price, but that amounted to nearly $1 million.

The two properties listed for sale in Burnaby last year both went through to completion.

The minutes from the tax sale show the same person purchased both properties.

An empty 9,262-square-foot lot on Walker Avenue sold for the upset price of $845, while its assessed value is $37,700.

The other property, which had an upset price of $269, was sold to the same buyer for $5,000. That may be less of a bargain — the property measures just 94-square feet and has a valuation of $3,600.

The City of Burnaby confirmed both properties were transferred after the one-year redemption period expired.

The City of Kelowna said it had an average of "about three to four properties" sold at its auction over the past six years, but added that "actual transfers of ownership through this process are very rare."

"City staff recall the last transfer occurring around 2016/2017," a spokeswoman said in a statement.

Abbotsford did not auction any properties this year or in 2024, but in 2025, it had two properties on the block. One sale went through on what the city called "a small undeveloped piece of land."

The highest bidders from Wednesday's auction in Vancouver must pay the upset price by noon Thursday.

Holden said bidders need to be prepared for their money to be tied up for a while, noting that while a six per cent interest rate may be enticing, most owners end up paying their taxes.

"Certainly, it's a way to put pressure on people to pay those outstanding taxes, and that's basically the function of it, for what it's worth," he said.

That seems to be the case for the property on Windsor Street, where a man who identified himself as the owner exited the house, causing the entire structure to rattle as he closed the door.

The resident, who declined to give his name, said he was aware his home was going on the auction block.

The property was, he said, his family home, while acknowledging that its ramshackle condition made living there "a challenge."

But he brushed off any concern about it being sold out from under him.

"I have a year to pay it," he said of his tax bill.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 4, 2026.

Brieanna Charlebois, The Canadian Press
